Synthesis and discussion

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
Lecture 1 established the Carhart four-factor model as the standard benchmark for evaluating equity fund performance. A natural follow-up question is: once we estimate alpha, how do we know whether it reflects skill or simply luck?
This lecture digs into three papers on this question:

Fama and French (2010): Use bootstrap simulations to separate luck from skill in the cross-section of mutual fund alphas. Their sobering conclusion: for net returns, few funds have sufficient skill to cover their costs.
Berk and van Binsbergen (2015): Reframe the question entirely. Instead of asking whether alpha is positive, they ask how much dollar value a fund extracts from markets. Their finding: the average fund adds roughly $3.2 million per year—but competition drives net returns to investors toward zero.
Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019): Ask a prior question—can these tests detect skill even when it is there? They show that the false discovery rate (FDR) methodology, a leading alternative to the bootstrap, misclassifies most genuinely skilled managers as having zero alpha, because fund returns are too noisy for the underlying tests to have power.

Together, the first two papers reveal a fundamental tension in the fund performance literature:

Skill exists (Berk & van Binsbergen), but investors cannot easily capture it (Fama & French).

The third paper adds a methodological warning that cuts across both:

A finding of “no skill” may be a finding about our instruments rather than about managers.

We will:

Understand the equilibrium accounting framework for evaluating fund performance in aggregate
Master the bootstrap simulation methodology for distinguishing luck from skill
Examine the false discovery rate approach and why Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) argue it fails in this setting
Learn the value-added measure of skill and why it differs from alpha
Examine the Berk-Green (2004) model and its empirical predictions
Implement a simplified bootstrap exercise in R using CRSP-style mutual fund data, and simulate the power problem directly

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
1. Motivation: The Luck-vs.-Skill Problem
Suppose you observe a fund with a four-factor alpha of +2% per year over 10 years. Should you conclude the manager is skilled? Not necessarily. With thousands of funds, some will have high alphas purely by chance. The core challenge is:
\[\underbrace{\hat{\alpha}_i}_{\text{estimated}} = \underbrace{\alpha_i}_{\text{true skill}} + \underbrace{\text{noise}}_{\text{estimation error}}\]
The noise component is not small. The average standard error of a fund’s monthly alpha estimate is about 0.28% per month (roughly 3.4% annualized), as documented by Fama and French (2010). With only 10 years of data (120 monthly observations), detecting a true annual alpha of 2% at the 5% significance level requires:
\[t = \frac{\hat{\alpha}}{\hat{\sigma}/\sqrt{T}} = \frac{2\%/12}{3.4\%/\sqrt{120}} \approx 0.63\]
This is far below the conventional threshold of 2.0. Statistical power is the central problem in evaluating individual fund performance—a point that Wermers (2011) emphasizes and that Lecture 1 introduced.






Important



Hold on to this calculation. In Section 4.5 we will see that Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) build an entire critique of the modern skill-measurement literature out of exactly this arithmetic. The low-power problem is not a caveat to be noted and set aside; it can reverse the economic conclusion.



Two Fundamental Questions
Fama and French (2010) and Berk and Binsbergen (2015) answer different but complementary questions:

Two perspectives on fund performance







Question
Fama & French (2010)
Berk & van Binsbergen (2015)




Unit of analysis
Return to investors
Dollar value extracted from markets


Measure of skill
Net / gross alpha
Value added = AUM × gross excess return


Key finding
Few funds cover costs
Average fund adds $3.2M/year


Conclusion on skill
Largely absent (net of fees)
Widespread; investors recognize it

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
2. Equilibrium Accounting (Fama & French 2010)

2.1 The Zero-Sum Identity
Fama and French (2010) begin with a powerful accounting constraint called equilibrium accounting. The aggregate of all investors holds the market portfolio. If passive investors hold passive strategies with zero alpha, then the aggregate portfolio of active investors must also have zero alpha—before costs.
This is essentially Sharpe’s Arithmetic (Sharpe 1991):
\[\underbrace{\alpha_{\text{active, aggregate}}}_{\text{must be zero (before costs)}} = 0\]
After costs:
\[\alpha_{\text{active, aggregate}}^{\text{net}} = -\text{expense ratio} < 0\]
Implication: Active management is a zero-sum game before costs and a negative-sum game after costs. If some funds have positive net alpha, other funds must have an equally large negative net alpha.


2.2 Aggregate Portfolio Results
Fama and French (2010) estimate regression (1) for the value-weighted (VW) and equal-weighted (EW) portfolios of all actively managed U.S. equity mutual funds, 1984–2006:
\[R_{i,t} - R_{f,t} = a_i + b_i(R_{M,t} - R_{f,t}) + s_i \text{SMB}_t + h_i \text{HML}_t + m_i \text{MOM}_t + e_{i,t} \tag{1}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
3. Bootstrap Simulation Methodology
The central methodological contribution of Fama and French (2010) is the bootstrap simulation approach to distinguishing luck from skill in the cross-section of fund alphas.

3.1 The Problem with Standard Inference
With thousands of funds, standard t-tests for individual fund alphas are unreliable for two reasons:

Multiple comparisons: With 3,000+ funds, many will have extreme alpha estimates purely by chance.
Cross-fund correlation: Fund returns are correlated (they hold similar stocks), so the cross-sectional distribution of t-statistics differs from the t-distribution assumed by standard tests.



3.2 The Bootstrap Procedure
Fama and French (2010) implement the following procedure:
Step 1 — Demean to impose zero true alpha:
For each fund \(i\), subtract its estimated alpha from its monthly returns to create “zero-alpha” returns: \[r_{i,t}^* = r_{i,t} - \hat{\alpha}_i\]
Step 2 — Bootstrap:
Draw a random sample (with replacement) of 273 months from the actual calendar months. Apply the same random draw to all funds simultaneously. This preserves: - The cross-correlation structure of fund returns - The time-series properties of explanatory returns (market, SMB, HML, MOM)
Step 3 — Estimate alphas on simulated data:
Run the four-factor regression for each fund on the simulated return series. Record the t-statistic \(t(\hat{\alpha})\) for each fund.
Step 4 — Repeat 10,000 times:
Build the distribution of \(t(\hat{\alpha})\) under the null hypothesis of zero true alpha.
Step 5 — Compare:
Compare the actual cross-section of \(t(\hat{\alpha})\) from real fund data to the simulated distribution. If the actual right tail is significantly fatter than the simulated right tail, this is evidence of genuine skill.


3.3 Why Joint Sampling Matters
A crucial feature of the Fama and French (2010) approach is that they draw the same random months for all funds. This is in contrast to Kosowski et al. (2006), who simulate each fund independently. Joint sampling matters because:

It preserves the correlation of alpha estimates across funds
It captures any correlated heteroskedasticity
It prevents false evidence of skill that arises from ignoring cross-fund dependence

Fama and French (2010) show that when Kosowski et al.’s stronger results are re-examined using joint sampling, the evidence for skill in the right tail weakens considerably.

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
4. Bootstrap Results: Luck vs. Skill

4.1 Net Returns: Few Managers Cover Costs
Fama and French (2010)’s main result on net returns is sobering. The cross-section of t(α) estimates from actual fund returns lies almost entirely to the left of the simulated distribution:

Below the 80th percentile, actual net return t(α) beats the simulated values in less than 1% of simulation runs
Even at the 90th percentile, 90% of simulations beat the actual t(α)

Interpretation: Most funds do not have sufficient skill to cover their costs. A fund at the 90th percentile of historical t(α)—which superficially looks very good—is in fact consistent with luck, not skill.
The one glimmer of hope: at the 97th–99th percentiles, the actual t(α) estimates are roughly in line with the simulated distribution. This suggests a small number of truly skilled managers exist, but they are hidden among lucky underperformers.


4.2 Gross Returns: Skill Exists, but Is Modest
When returns are measured gross of expenses, evidence of both positive and negative skill emerges:

Left tail: Actual t(α) is more extreme than simulated → evidence of truly unskilled managers who produce negative alpha before fees
Right tail: Actual t(α) exceeds simulated values → evidence of genuinely skilled managers who outperform passive benchmarks before fees

Fama and French (2010) quantify the cross-sectional dispersion of true alpha using additional simulations with injected alpha. Their estimate:
\[\sigma(\alpha^{\text{true}}) \approx 1.25\% \text{ per year}\]
This is a normal distribution with mean zero. Implications:

Roughly 16% of funds have true gross alpha > 1.25% per year (≈10 bp/month)
Only 2.4% have true gross alpha > 2.50% per year (≈21 bp/month)







Important



The skill that exists is not large enough to cover costs for most managers. A true gross alpha of 1.25% barely covers a 1% expense ratio. After fees, most skilled managers produce approximately zero alpha for investors.




4.3 Graphical Summary: The CDF Comparison
The key figure in Fama and French (2010) compares the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of actual vs. simulated t(α):

For net returns: The actual CDF lies to the left of the simulated CDF almost everywhere → negative skill overall
For gross returns: The actual CDF crosses the simulated CDF around the 60th–70th percentile → positive skill in the right tail, negative skill in the left tail



4.4 A Competing Route: The False Discovery Rate
The bootstrap tells us whether the tails of the cross-section look unusual, but it does not directly tell us what fraction of funds have positive, zero, or negative alpha. Barras et al. (2010)—hereafter BSW—propose an approach that does: the false discovery rate (FDR), imported from the multiple-testing literature in statistics (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995).
The logic is elegant. Run a separate alpha test for every fund and collect the \(I\) p-values \(\hat{p}_i\). Under the null of zero alpha, a p-value is uniform on \([0,1]\). So if we pick a high threshold \(\lambda\)—say 0.5—and assume that every p-value above \(\lambda\) comes from a genuinely zero-alpha fund, we can count those p-values and extrapolate to the whole interval:
\[\hat{\pi}^0(\lambda) = \frac{\frac{1}{1-\lambda} \cdot \#\{\hat{p}_i : \hat{p}_i > \lambda\}}{I} \tag{2}\]
Knowing \(\hat{\pi}^0\), we can then take the funds that did reject at some significance level \(\gamma\), subtract the number we expect to have rejected by luck alone (\(\hat{\pi}^0 \cdot \gamma\)), and recover the proportions of truly negative- and positive-alpha funds:
\[\hat{\pi}^-(\gamma,\lambda) = \frac{\#\{(\hat{\alpha}_i,\hat{p}_i) : \hat{\alpha}_i < 0,\ \hat{p}_i < \gamma\}}{I} - \hat{\pi}^0(\lambda)\cdot\frac{\gamma}{2} \tag{3a}\]
\[\hat{\pi}^+(\gamma,\lambda) = \frac{\#\{(\hat{\alpha}_i,\hat{p}_i) : \hat{\alpha}_i > 0,\ \hat{p}_i < \gamma\}}{I} - \hat{\pi}^0(\lambda)\cdot\frac{\gamma}{2} \tag{3b}\]
Applied to U.S. equity mutual funds, BSW report that 75% of funds have zero alpha net of expenses, 24.4% have negative alpha, and only 0.6% have positive alpha. These numbers have been enormously influential. They are read as direct confirmation of Berk and Green (2004): if almost every fund sits at exactly zero net alpha, that is what a competitive equilibrium with rational capital reallocation looks like.
The method spread well beyond mutual funds—to hedge funds, trading strategies, takeover announcements, and jump detection in asset returns.


4.5 Reassessing the FDR: Skill, Luck, or Lack of Power?
Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) ask whether the FDR can actually do what it claims in this setting. Their answer is no, and the reason is the arithmetic from Section 1.
Look again at equation (2). It rests on an assumption that is easy to miss: every p-value above \(\lambda\) belongs to a zero-alpha fund. That holds only if nonzero alphas are large relative to their standard errors—in other words, only if the individual tests have power. If a fund has a real alpha of 1% per year but its alpha is estimated with a standard error of comparable size, its p-value is essentially a draw from the uniform distribution too. It lands above \(\lambda\) roughly as often as a genuinely zero-alpha fund’s would, and the FDR counts it as one.
The bias runs in one direction. Because equation (2) divides by \(1-\lambda\), each skilled fund that fails to reject contributes \(1/(1-\lambda) = 2\) funds to the zero-alpha tally when \(\lambda = 0.5\). The FDR systematically overstates the proportion of zero-alpha funds and understates the proportion with genuine skill.






ImportantThe headline result



Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) find that, at the sample sizes actually available in mutual fund data, the FDR misclassifies as zero-alpha:

90% of funds whose true alpha is ±1% per year
65% of funds whose true alpha is ±2% per year
roughly 30% of funds whose true alpha is as large as ±3.5% per year

A 2% annual alpha is not a rounding error. It is roughly twice the average expense ratio, and a manager who reliably delivered it would be a star. The methodology cannot see two-thirds of them.



Why BSW’s own simulation looked so convincing
BSW validated the FDR with a simulation, and in that simulation it performed beautifully. Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) show why: the simulation was run under conditions far more favorable than the real data.

Why the BSW simulation overstates FDR accuracy






BSW simulation assumption
Reality in mutual fund data




Nonzero alphas at −3.2% and +3.8% per year
Large share of funds have alphas between 1% and 2.5%


\(T = 384\) months per fund (the maximum in the data)
Median 150, mean 180 observations per fund


\(N = 1{,}400\) funds, balanced panel
2,076 funds, unbalanced panel


Little or no cross-sectional error correlation
Substantial correlation from common strategies



Each of these pushes in the same direction. The result is that a methodology which looks nearly unbiased in its original validation becomes badly biased once the data-generating process resembles the data it is applied to.


Three findings that make this hard to fix
More funds do not help. This is the most counterintuitive result. Increasing \(N\) leaves the bias essentially unchanged, because \(N\) affects neither the power of each individual test nor the distribution of p-values. Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) put it memorably: it is like estimating a population’s mean weight by weighing more and more people on a biased scale. Only \(T\)—observations per fund—matters, and convergence is glacial. They find that even 200 years of monthly data would not be enough to get accurate estimates for realistic alpha distributions.
Confidence intervals are not a safety net. For roughly half the data-generating processes they examine, the nominal 95% confidence intervals around the FDR estimates never contain the true proportions across 1,000 simulated samples. Realistic cross-sectional correlation in residuals inflates the estimator’s variability by about a factor of five, widening 90% intervals by 4.6 to 7.5 times.
The correction may not beat no correction. For alphas of 1% or 2% per year, the FDR does not outperform the naive “no-luck” approach of simply counting significant alphas without any multiple-testing adjustment—and can do worse, because its bias is so large.


The connection back to Fama and French
There is a result here that speaks directly to Section 4.2. Recall that Fama and French (2010) estimate the cross-sectional dispersion of true alpha at about 1.25% per year. Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) simulate a data-generating process calibrated close to that estimate—alphas drawn from a normal with \(\sigma_\alpha = 1.5\%\), with only 1% of funds having exactly zero alpha—and apply the FDR to it. The FDR reports that 70% of funds have zero alpha.
In other words: take the world that Fama and French’s own estimates describe, and the FDR will tell you it is the world that BSW found.






NoteWhat this does and does not overturn



Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) is a critique of a methodology, not a claim that mutual fund managers are secretly skilled. They do not estimate skill themselves in this paper. What they establish is that the widely cited “75% of funds have zero alpha” figure cannot bear the economic weight placed on it—in particular, it is not evidence for the Berk and Green (2004) equilibrium, because an estimator with this much bias would report approximately that number whether or not Berk-Green were true.
A test that returns the same answer under the hypothesis and its negation is not evidence about the hypothesis.




What to do instead
The authors are constructive. Their recommendations:

Check power before trusting the estimator. Simulate your own data-generating process and verify that individual tests have enough power for the FDR’s assumptions to hold. This is cheap—we do it in Section 10.
Pool cross-sectional information rather than testing each fund in isolation. Approaches that estimate the whole cross-sectional distribution of alpha, rather than running \(I\) separate underpowered tests, extract far more from the same data. They point to Harvey and Liu (2018) and their own related work in this vein.
Be wary of the FDR wherever the signal-to-noise ratio is low. The problem is not specific to mutual funds. Any application with large \(N\) and small \(T\)—hedge funds, trading strategies, event studies—inherits it.

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
5. The Value-Added Approach (Berk & van Binsbergen 2015)

5.1 Why Alpha Fails as a Skill Measure
Berk and Binsbergen (2015) make a fundamental theoretical point: neither net alpha nor gross alpha correctly measures managerial skill. The argument proceeds as follows.
Under standard neoclassical assumptions (rational investors, competitive markets, optimizing managers with decreasing returns to scale):
Net alpha measures market efficiency, not skill. If investors are rational and markets competitive, the net alpha is driven to zero by capital flows—regardless of skill. A fund with high skill attracts capital until its net alpha is competed away.
Gross alpha equals the fee the manager charges. To see this, note: \[\alpha^{\text{gross}} = \alpha^{\text{net}} + f_i = 0 + f_i = f_i\]
where \(f_i\) is the fund’s percentage fee. The gross alpha is a choice variable of the manager, not a measure of skill. A manager who indexes more of the portfolio can achieve any desired gross alpha by adjusting the fee accordingly.
This leads to a striking proposition (Berk & van Binsbergen 2015, Proposition 1):

The only condition under which gross alpha measures managerial skill is if all managers set their fees to ensure that the AUM of all funds is exactly $1.

Since AUM varies enormously across funds, gross alpha is an unreliable proxy for skill in practice (their Table 8: cross-sectional correlation between value added and gross alpha is only 23%, with \(R^2 = 5\%\)).


5.2 The Value-Added Measure
The correct measure of managerial skill, according to Berk and Binsbergen (2015), is the value added of the fund—the dollar value extracted from financial markets:
\[V_{i,t} = q_{i,t-1} \cdot (R_{i,t}^g - R_{i,t}^B) \tag{4}\]
where: - \(q_{i,t-1}\) = assets under management (AUM) at the end of the prior period - \(R_{i,t}^g\) = gross excess return of fund \(i\) at time \(t\) - \(R_{i,t}^B\) = benchmark return (the investor’s next best alternative)
The fund’s skill is the time-series expectation of value added: \[S_i \equiv \mathbb{E}[V_{i,t}] \tag{5}\]
Intuitively: a manager who adds 1% alpha on a $10 billion fund adds more value ($100 million) than a manager who adds 10% alpha on a $1 million fund ($100,000), even though the former has a much lower gross alpha.






Tip



Notice that the value-added measure sidesteps part of the problem Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) identify. Dollar value added is estimated from the level of AUM times realized excess return, and its cross-sectional dispersion is enormous, so the signal-to-noise ratio is far better than it is for percentage alpha. This is one reason Berk and Binsbergen (2015) can document persistence over ten years where alpha-based studies find almost none.




5.3 The Benchmark: Vanguard Index Funds
A critical design choice in Berk and Binsbergen (2015) is the benchmark. The standard approach (Carhart four factors) uses factor-mimicking portfolios that:

Were not actually available to investors in the early part of the sample (e.g., small-cap and value index funds were not widely available until the early 1990s)
Do not account for transaction costs
May contain hindsight bias

Berk and Binsbergen (2015) instead use Vanguard index funds as the benchmark—the actual investment opportunity available to investors at each point in time. This benchmark:

Is guaranteed to be tradable and marketed
Includes transaction costs
Reflects the dynamic evolution of available passive strategies

The FFC (Fama-French-Carhart) factor portfolios themselves produce significantly positive alpha relative to Vanguard benchmarks:

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
6. The Berk-Green (2004) Model
Both papers reference the theoretical framework of Berk and Green (2004), which provides an equilibrium model of the mutual fund industry. The key predictions of the model:

Fund managers have skill (positive gross alpha on the first dollar managed)
Decreasing returns to scale: the more capital a manager actively manages, the lower the alpha per dollar
Rational investors: capital flows to funds with positive expected alpha until expected net alpha is driven to zero
In equilibrium: every fund has zero net alpha, but managers capture all economic rents through fees

This model has three testable predictions that the papers address:

Testing the Berk-Green (2004) model








Prediction
Fama & French (2010)
Berk & van Binsbergen (2015)
Andrikogiannopoulou & Papakonstantinou (2019)




Zero net alpha in aggregate
Rejected: aggregate net alpha ≈ −1%/year
Not directly tested; focus on value added
Not tested directly


Investors identify and reward skill
Not examined
Confirmed: current compensation predicts future value added
Not examined


Most individual funds have zero alpha
Consistent with bootstrap evidence
Not the right question
Cannot be inferred from FDR estimates: the estimator would report this regardless



Fama and French (2010) explicitly state that their results “reject most of [Berk and Green’s] predictions about mutual fund returns.” The aggregate negative net alpha contradicts the model’s prediction that all managers have zero expected net alpha in equilibrium.
Berk and Binsbergen (2015) find results more consistent with Berk-Green: investors do appear to identify skilled managers (compensation predicts future value added), and the cross-sectional distribution of skill is persistent for up to ten years.
Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) add a third position that is neither support nor rejection: the FDR evidence most often cited in favor of Berk-Green is uninformative about it, so the model’s empirical status rests on the other two literatures rather than on the “75% zero alpha” statistic.

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
7. Key Results: Berk & van Binsbergen (2015)

7.1 Average Fund Adds Positive Value
Using the Vanguard benchmark, the average mutual fund adds approximately $3.2 million per year (time-weighted mean: $270,000/month in Y2000 dollars). The t-statistic is 5.74—strong statistical evidence against the no-skill hypothesis.
Using the FFC risk adjustment, the result is similar: $250,000/month, t = 3.94.
However, the distribution is highly skewed:

Distribution of value added across funds (Berk & van Binsbergen 2015, Table 3)


Percentile

% with positive value added

Most funds destroy value; the average is positive because the minority of skilled managers manages most of the capital.


7.2 Persistence of Value Added
The most compelling evidence for skill is the persistence of value added for up to 10 years. Berk and Binsbergen (2015) construct a non-parametric test: do funds in the top decile (by skill ratio) continue to beat funds in the bottom decile in future periods?
The null hypothesis is Binomial(n, ½): under no skill, top decile funds beat bottom decile funds 50% of the time. The actual results:

Top decile beats bottom decile at every horizon from 3 to 10 years
The null is rejected at the 95% confidence level at most horizons
The top decile controls approximately 25% of total AUM (investors reward skill with capital)

This persistence is far longer than anything documented using alpha measures, which Carhart (1997) and others have found to be largely unpredictable.


7.3 Investors Can Identify Skill
A surprising finding: current managerial compensation predicts future value added better than past value added does. This means investors are not “dumb money” chasing past returns—they appear to genuinely infer managerial skill and allocate capital accordingly.
Managerial compensation = AUM × fee rate. Since fee rates vary little across funds, it is primarily investors’ capital allocation decisions that determine compensation. The finding implies that the flow-performance relationship reflects rational information processing, consistent with Berk and Green (2004).


7.4 Where Does the Value Go?
Value added can be decomposed into:
\[V_{i,t} = \underbrace{q_{i,t-1} \cdot f_{i,t-1}}_{\text{fees (compensation)}} + \underbrace{q_{i,t-1} \cdot \varepsilon_{i,t}}_{\text{returns to investors}}\]
Berk and Binsbergen (2015) find that the net alpha to investors is approximately zero—managers capture essentially all economic rents through fees. Investors receive no abnormal return from investing in skilled funds because competition drives net alpha to zero. This is the central prediction of Berk and Green (2004), and it is confirmed by the data.
Furthermore, roughly half of total value added comes from diversification services (the value Vanguard itself charges for) and half from active stock picking and market timing.

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
8. Reconciling the Three Papers
A reader might be confused: Fama & French say skill is rare; Berk & van Binsbergen say the average fund is skilled; Andrikogiannopoulou & Papakonstantinou say we may not be able to tell. Who is right?
All three are right—they are answering different questions:

Reconciling the three papers








Dimension
Fama & French (2010)
Berk & van Binsbergen (2015)
Andrikogiannopoulou & Papakonstantinou (2019)




Skill exists?
Modest evidence (gross returns only)
Yes—average fund adds $3.2M/year
Unanswerable from FDR estimates


Do investors benefit?
No—net returns are negative
No—net alpha ≈ 0 (rents captured by managers)
Not addressed


Can investors identify skilled funds?
Not examined
Yes—compensation predicts future value added
Not addressed


Right benchmark?
FFC factors
Vanguard index funds (preferred)
Not addressed


Can the test detect skill?
Bootstrap has some power in the tails
Value added has far better signal-to-noise
No—FDR misses 65% of ±2% alphas



The substantive resolution between the first two:

Skill exists and is measurable in dollars. But competition among investors drives the net return to investors to zero. Skilled managers capture all rents through fees and fund size. The dollar evidence of skill is clear; the return evidence is weak because rational flows eliminate the return opportunity.

And the methodological caution the third paper adds:

Before interpreting any “no skill” finding, ask what the test would have reported had skill been present. If the answer is “the same thing,” the finding is about the test.

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
9. Implications for Practice

9.1 For Performance Evaluation

Do not rely on alpha alone. The cross-section of alpha estimates is dominated by noise. Only the extreme tails (99th percentile and beyond) provide any reliable signal of genuine skill after accounting for multiple comparisons.
Consider fund size. Berk & van Binsbergen demonstrate that small funds can have high alpha but low value added. A large fund with modest alpha may be adding more value in dollar terms.
Use the right benchmark. FFC factors contain hindsight bias. Traded alternatives (passive index funds) are a more appropriate benchmark for evaluating whether a manager beats the investor’s actual opportunity set.



9.2 For Investors

The expected net return from active management is approximately zero or slightly negative. Fama & French’s equilibrium accounting tells us this must be true on average. The zero or negative net alpha is not a measurement artifact.
Identifying skilled managers is difficult but not impossible. Berk & van Binsbergen show that investors in aggregate appear to do so (compensation predicts performance). But individual investors face a severe information disadvantage relative to the institutional investors who dominate capital flows.
Passive investing dominates for most investors. Even if skill exists and is persistent, skilled managers capture their own rents. Net alpha to investors is approximately zero for the best funds—and negative for most funds.



9.3 For Research

Bootstrap simulation is the gold standard for detecting skill in cross-sections of fund returns. Standard t-tests are inadequate due to multiple comparisons and cross-fund correlation.
Statistical power is severely limited with typical mutual fund sample sizes. A fund needs decades of monthly data to reliably distinguish a 2% annual alpha from noise. For shorter-lived funds, inference requires simulation-based methods.
Validate your estimator on a realistic DGP, not a convenient one (Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou 2019). BSW’s validation simulation was internally correct; it simply assumed alphas far larger and panels far longer than the data contain. Before adopting any estimator, simulate it under parameters calibrated to the data you actually have.
Adding observations in the cross-section does not fix a power problem. Power depends on \(T\) per unit, not \(N\). This is worth internalizing: it applies to panel settings throughout empirical finance, not just fund performance.

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
10. Empirical Implementation
In this section we implement a simplified version of the Fama and French (2010) bootstrap procedure. We use the same 10 US ETFs and factor data from Lecture 1 to illustrate the methodology. Note that this exercise is pedagogical—the full Fama and French (2010) analysis uses thousands of actively managed mutual funds.

Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyquant)
library(frenchdata)
library(broom)
library(gt)
library(scales)

set.seed(42)  # reproducibility




Load Data from Lecture 1


Code
# --- ETF list and labels ---
etf_tickers <- c("SPY","QQQ","IWM","VTV","VUG","ARKK","XLE","XLF","VNQ","IWD")
etf_labels  <- tibble(
  symbol   = etf_tickers,
  name     = c("S&P 500","Nasdaq-100","Russell 2000","Vanguard Value",
               "Vanguard Growth","ARK Innovation","Energy Sector",
               "Financials Sector","Real Estate (REIT)","Russell 1000 Value"),
  category = c("Broad market","Tech/Growth","Small cap","Large value",
               "Large growth","Active growth","Sector","Sector","REIT","Large value")
)

# --- Download prices ---
start_date <- "2015-01-01"
end_date   <- "2024-12-31"

prices_raw <- tq_get(etf_tickers, from = start_date, to = end_date,
                     get = "stock.prices")

# --- Monthly returns ---
returns_monthly <- prices_raw |>
  group_by(symbol) |>
  tq_transmute(select = adjusted, mutate_fun = periodReturn,
               period = "monthly", type = "arithmetic",
               col_rename = "ret") |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(etf_labels, by = "symbol")

# --- French factors ---
ff3_raw  <- download_french_data("Fama/French 3 Factors")
mom_raw  <- download_french_data("Momentum Factor (Mom)")

ff3_monthly <- ff3_raw$subsets$data[[1]] |>
  mutate(date = lubridate::ym(date),
         across(c(`Mkt-RF`, SMB, HML, RF), ~ . / 100)) |>
  rename(RMRF = `Mkt-RF`) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date(start_date), date <= as.Date(end_date))

mom_monthly <- mom_raw$subsets$data[[1]] |>
  mutate(date = lubridate::ym(date), Mom = Mom / 100) |>
  rename(UMD = Mom) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date(start_date), date <= as.Date(end_date))

factors <- left_join(ff3_monthly, mom_monthly, by = "date")

# --- Merge and compute excess returns ---
data_merged <- returns_monthly |>
  mutate(ym = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  left_join(factors |> mutate(ym = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>
              select(ym, RMRF, SMB, HML, UMD, RF),
            by = "ym") |>
  mutate(excess_ret = ret - RF) |>
  filter(!is.na(RMRF))

data_merged |>
  select(symbol, ym, excess_ret, RMRF, SMB, HML, UMD) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

Step 2 — Impose Zero Alpha (Demean Returns)


Code
# Subtract estimated alpha from each fund's excess returns
# This creates the population from which we bootstrap
data_zero_alpha <- data_merged |>
  left_join(carhart_base |> select(symbol, alpha_estimate), by = "symbol") |>
  mutate(excess_ret_zero = excess_ret - alpha_estimate)

# Quick check: every fund's alpha on demeaned returns should be ~0.
# Report the worst case across funds, not an average — an average could
# hide two large errors of opposite sign.
data_zero_alpha |>
  group_by(symbol) |>
  do(tidy(lm(excess_ret_zero ~ RMRF + SMB + HML + UMD, data = .))) |>
  filter(term == "(Intercept)") |>
  ungroup() |>
  summarise(max_abs_intercept = max(abs(estimate))) |>
  pull(max_abs_intercept)   # should be ~1e-18


[1] 1.97132e-17




Step 3 — Bootstrap Simulation
We draw 1,000 random samples of months (with replacement), applying the same draw to all ETFs to preserve cross-correlation. For each draw, we estimate the four-factor model and record the t-statistic for alpha.
The implementation below arranges the data as two matrices once, then resamples rows. This is worth doing carefully, because the structure of the code is the methodological point of Fama and French (2010): a single index vector idx is applied to the factor matrix and the fund matrix simultaneously, so every fund sees the same calendar months in the same order. Independent per-fund sampling — the Kosowski et al. (2006) approach — would require drawing a separate idx inside the fund loop, which is exactly the one-line change that destroys the cross-correlation structure.


Code
# Funds as columns, months as rows. Keep only months where every fund
# has data, so the joint draw is well defined.
wide_rets <- data_zero_alpha |>
  select(symbol, ym, excess_ret_zero) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = symbol, values_from = excess_ret_zero) |>
  arrange(ym) |>
  drop_na()

wide_facs <- data_zero_alpha |>
  distinct(ym, RMRF, SMB, HML, UMD) |>
  arrange(ym) |>
  semi_join(wide_rets, by = "ym")

stopifnot(identical(wide_facs$ym, wide_rets$ym))

fund_cols <- setdiff(names(wide_rets), "ym")

Y <- as.matrix(wide_rets[, fund_cols])              # T x N  fund returns
X <- cbind(`(Intercept)` = 1,
           as.matrix(wide_facs[, c("RMRF", "SMB", "HML", "UMD")]))  # T x 5

cat("Bootstrap panel:", nrow(Y), "months x", ncol(Y), "funds\n")


Bootstrap panel: 120 months x 10 funds




Code
# t(alpha) for ALL funds at once, given a design matrix and return matrix.
# Vectorised across funds: one solve() per simulation rather than one
# lm() per fund. Verified to reproduce summary(lm(...)) to ~1e-12.
alpha_tstats <- function(X, Y) {
  XtXinv <- solve(crossprod(X))
  B      <- XtXinv %*% crossprod(X, Y)            # 5 x N coefficients
  resid  <- Y - X %*% B
  sigma2 <- colSums(resid^2) / (nrow(X) - ncol(X))
  B[1, ] / sqrt(XtXinv[1, 1] * sigma2)            # intercept t-stats
}




Code
n_sim <- 1000        # full paper uses 10,000; 1,000 runs in about a second
n_obs <- nrow(Y)

sim_t_stats <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_sim, ncol = ncol(Y),
                      dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(Y)))

for (b in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  # ONE index vector, applied to factors and every fund alike.
  # This is what "joint sampling" means in Fama-French (2010).
  idx <- sample.int(n_obs, size = n_obs, replace = TRUE)
  sim_t_stats[b, ] <- alpha_tstats(X[idx, , drop = FALSE],
                                   Y[idx, , drop = FALSE])
}

sim_t_df <- as_tibble(sim_t_stats) |>
  mutate(sim = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-sim, names_to = "symbol", values_to = "t_sim")

  summarise(

  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50,
                 fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = t_actual), color = "tomato",

Simulating the Value-Added Measure
To illustrate the Berk and Binsbergen (2015) approach, we compute a simplified value-added measure for each ETF. We proxy AUM using the ETF’s market price × shares outstanding—not directly available via tidyquant, so we demonstrate with hypothetical but plausible AUM data.


Code
# Use hypothetical (approximate) average AUM for each ETF (in billions USD)
# These are rough approximations for pedagogical illustration
aum_proxy <- tibble(
  symbol = etf_tickers,
  avg_aum_bn = c(500, 250, 70, 100, 120, 10, 25, 40, 65, 55)  # approximate 2015-2024 avg AUM
)

# Compute value added: AUM × gross excess return above RMRF benchmark
# Here we use RMRF as the naive one-factor benchmark for illustration
value_added <- data_merged |>
  left_join(aum_proxy, by = "symbol") |>
  mutate(
    # Simplified value added: AUM * (fund return - market return benchmark)
    # In practice, BvB use the Vanguard multi-fund benchmark
    gross_excess_vs_mkt = excess_ret - RMRF,
    value_added_mn = avg_aum_bn * 1000 * gross_excess_vs_mkt  # in $millions
  ) |>
  group_by(symbol, name) |>
  summarise(
    mean_va_ann  = mean(value_added_mn, na.rm = TRUE) * 12,   # annualized avg
    mean_alpha   = mean(excess_ret - RMRF, na.rm = TRUE) * 12,
    avg_aum_bn   = first(avg_aum_bn),
    .groups      = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_va_ann))

Illustrating the Power Problem
The exercises above take the estimator’s accuracy for granted. This one checks it. Following Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019), we build a world where we know the truth, run the FDR estimator on it, and see what it reports.
The setup is deliberately generous to the FDR. We assume alphas are estimated with no factor-model misspecification and no cross-sectional correlation in residuals—both of which, in the paper, make matters worse.


Code
# Parameters follow Andrikogiannopoulou & Papakonstantinou (2019):
# monthly residual SD of 0.021 in their baseline calibration, lambda = 0.5.
sigma_e <- 0.021
lambda  <- 0.5

# Simulate one cross-section of funds with KNOWN alphas, then apply the
# FDR estimator of equation (2) and return its estimate of pi^0.
fdr_pi0 <- function(n_funds, T_obs, pi0, pi_neg, pi_pos, alpha_bar) {
  se    <- sigma_e / sqrt(T_obs)      # SE of the monthly alpha estimate
  a_m   <- alpha_bar / 12             # annual alpha -> monthly
  truth <- sample(c(0, -a_m, a_m), n_funds, replace = TRUE,
                  prob = c(pi0, pi_neg, pi_pos))
  ahat  <- rnorm(n_funds, mean = truth, sd = se)
  pval  <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(ahat / se)))
  mean(pval > lambda) / (1 - lambda)  # equation (2)
}




Code
set.seed(2019)

fdr_grid <- expand_grid(
  alpha_bar = c(0.010, 0.020, 0.035),
  T_obs     = c(180, 384)
) |>
  mutate(
    pi0_hat = map2_dbl(alpha_bar, T_obs, \(a, t)
      mean(replicate(200, fdr_pi0(2000, t, 0.75, 0.23, 0.02, a)))),
    bias = pi0_hat - 0.75
  )

fdr_grid |>
  mutate(T_lab = if_else(T_obs == 180,
                         "T = 180 (data median/mean)",
                         "T = 384 (BSW simulation)")) |>
  select(T_lab, alpha_bar, pi0_hat, bias) |>
  arrange(T_lab, alpha_bar) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "T_lab") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(alpha_bar, pi0_hat, bias), decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(
    alpha_bar = "True |α| of nonzero funds (ann.)",
    pi0_hat   = "FDR estimate of π⁰",

Read the bottom row of each block first. With \(T = 384\) and alphas of ±3.5% per year—BSW’s simulation design—the FDR recovers a \(\pi^0\) of about 76% against a truth of 75%. The estimator looks excellent, which is exactly what BSW reported.
Now read upward. Holding everything else fixed and shrinking the true alpha to ±1% per year, the same estimator reports that roughly 94% of funds have zero alpha. Nothing changed about the method; only the world it was applied to.


Code
misclass <- function(alpha_bar, T_obs) {
  se <- sigma_e / sqrt(T_obs)
  # P(p-value > lambda) for a fund whose true alpha is alpha_bar,
  # scaled by 1/(1-lambda) because equation (2) extrapolates.
  p_above <- pnorm(qnorm(1 - lambda / 2) - (alpha_bar / 12) / se)
  pmin(1, p_above / (1 - lambda))
}

expand_grid(
  alpha_bar = seq(0.005, 0.05, by = 0.001),
  T_obs     = c(120, 180, 384)
) |>
  mutate(
    rate  = misclass(alpha_bar, T_obs),
    T_lab = factor(T_obs, levels = c(120, 180, 384),
                   labels = c("T = 120", "T = 180 (realistic)", "T = 384"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(alpha_bar, rate, color = T_lab)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.01, 0.02), linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.0205, y = 0.05, hjust = 0, size = 3,
           label = "±1% and ±2% per year") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "True annual alpha of a nonzero-alpha fund",
    y = "Probability of being counted as zero-alpha",
    color = NULL,
    title = "Where the FDR loses skilled managers",
    subtitle = "Economically large alphas are invisible at realistic sample lengths"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Figure 2: Share of genuinely nonzero-alpha funds that the FDR classifies as zero-alpha











WarningHow closely does this match the paper?



Reasonably, but not exactly, and the gap is worth understanding.
Our simplified version draws \(\hat\alpha\) directly from a normal rather than estimating it from a factor regression, and it fixes \(\lambda = 0.5\) where Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) select \(\lambda\) optimally by bootstrap and average over 1,000 repetitions. It reproduces their central case closely—at \(T = 384\) with ±3.5% alphas we get \(\hat\pi^0 \approx 76\%\) against their reported 76.3%—but our misclassification rates for small alphas run somewhat higher than their simulated 90% and 65% figures.
Treat the exact numbers here as illustrative and the paper’s as authoritative. The mechanism, the sign of the bias, and its order of magnitude are what this exercise is for. The fact that a back-of-envelope reproduces the qualitative result is itself the point: the bias is not subtle, and anyone could have checked.

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
12. Key Takeaways

Equilibrium accounting constrains aggregate performance (Fama and French 2010). Before costs, aggregate active management must have zero alpha. After costs, it must be negative. This is arithmetic, not an empirical finding.
The bootstrap simulation is the right tool for separating luck from skill in large fund cross-sections. Standard t-tests fail due to multiple comparisons and cross-fund correlation. Joint resampling of months preserves the correlation structure of fund returns.
Few funds cover costs on net returns (Fama and French 2010). The cross-section of t(α) for net returns is almost entirely to the left of the simulated null distribution. Skill is detectable only in the extreme right tail (≥97th percentile) and even then the evidence is mixed.
Skill exists in gross returns, with true alpha dispersion of roughly ±1.25% per year. But this barely covers average expense ratios of 1%.
The FDR estimate that “75% of funds have zero alpha” does not survive scrutiny (Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou 2019). At realistic sample lengths the methodology misclassifies 65% of funds with alphas of ±2% per year, and 90% of those with ±1%. The bias is upward in \(\pi^0\) by construction, because equation (2) extrapolates every failure to reject.
Low power is not a caveat; it can invert the conclusion. Under a data-generating process calibrated to Fama and French’s own estimate of alpha dispersion—where only 1% of funds truly have zero alpha—the FDR reports 70% zero-alpha funds. An estimator that returns BSW’s answer whether or not BSW’s world obtains is not evidence for that world, and therefore not evidence for Berk and Green (2004) either.
Power comes from \(T\), not \(N\). Adding funds does not improve the FDR estimator at all; only lengthening each fund’s return history does, and convergence is so slow that even 200 years of monthly data would be insufficient. This generalizes well beyond fund performance.
Alpha is the wrong measure of skill (Berk and Binsbergen 2015). Under standard neoclassical assumptions, neither net alpha (driven to zero by competition) nor gross alpha (equals the manager’s chosen fee) measures skill. Value added—AUM times gross excess return—is the correct measure.
The average fund adds $3.2 million per year in dollar terms (Berk and Binsbergen 2015). Skill is widespread but concentrated among large funds. Cross-sectional differences in skill persist for up to 10 years—far longer than persistence in alpha.
Investors appear to identify skill: managerial compensation (AUM × fee) predicts future value added. Capital flows to skilled managers, consistent with Berk and Green (2004).
Skilled managers capture all rents: net alpha to investors is approximately zero even for the best funds. There is no free lunch in active management—the benefit of skill accrues to the manager, not the investor.

title: Lecture 2: Fund Performance, Skill, and Luck
text:
Discussion Questions

Fama and French (2010) find that the VW portfolio of active funds has a net alpha of approximately −1% per year. Is this evidence that active managers lack skill, or evidence that investors rationally drive net alphas to zero? How would you distinguish between these two interpretations empirically?
Berk and Binsbergen (2015) argue that gross alpha is not a valid measure of skill because it equals the fee the manager charges. Does this imply that a manager who charges 2% in fees is more skilled than one who charges 0.5%? What does the theory actually predict about the relationship between fees and skill?
The Fama and French (2010) bootstrap preserves cross-correlation by jointly sampling months for all funds. Why is this important? What would happen to the simulation results if each fund’s months were sampled independently?
Berk and Binsbergen (2015) use Vanguard index funds rather than FFC factors as the benchmark. Their Table 2 shows that HML and UMD have significant positive alpha relative to Vanguard funds. What does this imply about alpha estimates computed using FFC factors for the early part of the sample?
Suppose a fund manager has a true annual alpha of 2% and manages $100 million. Under the Berk-Green (2004) model, what happens to the fund’s alpha and AUM over time as investors observe the fund’s performance? Is this story consistent with Berk and Binsbergen (2015)’s finding that value-added persistence lasts 10 years?
Fama and French (2010) find that the CAPM (single-factor) bootstrap produces much stronger apparent evidence of skill than the four-factor bootstrap. Why does adding size, value, and momentum factors to the benchmark reduce the apparent evidence of skill? What does this tell you about the source of “alpha” in a CAPM regression?
Write down the assumption behind equation (2) in words, then state precisely when it fails. Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) show that the resulting bias in \(\hat\pi^0\) is always upward. Explain why the bias cannot go the other way, and why the factor \(1/(1-\lambda)\) makes it worse rather than better.
Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019) find that increasing the number of funds \(N\) does not reduce the FDR estimator’s bias, while increasing the number of observations per fund \(T\) does. Explain the asymmetry. Then consider: does the Fama and French (2010) bootstrap suffer from the same problem? Which features of the bootstrap make it more or less vulnerable than the FDR, and does it escape the low-power critique entirely?
Suppose you are refereeing a paper that applies the FDR methodology to a panel of 3,000 hedge funds with an average of 48 monthly return observations each. Using the reasoning in Andrikogiannopoulou and Papakonstantinou (2019), what would you ask the authors to demonstrate before you would believe their estimated proportions? Be specific about the simulation you would request.

title: Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
text:
1. Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(highcharter)   # interactive charts (no ggplot2 in this lecture)
library(gt)
library(quadprog)      # Sharpe (1992) style analysis
library(tidyquant)     # Yahoo Finance prices (style-drift section, §6.5)
library(frenchdata)    # Kenneth French's Data Library



1.1 Where does the fund data come from?
The CRSP Mutual Fund Database is licensed, so a public handout cannot ship it, and the results of this lecture cannot be shown on real CRSP data. Every chunk below therefore runs on a simulated CRSP-style panel with the same column names as the CRSP fund summary file (crsp_fundno, wficn, lipper_obj_cd, crsp_obj_cd, index_fund_flag, et_flag, tna_latest, exp_ratio, and so on). If you have WRDS access, the same code runs on your own extract once you replace simulate_crsp() with a loader that returns these columns.
Simulated data have one advantage that real data never have: we know the true type of every fund, so we can score each filter and each classification recipe against the truth.






TipCaching



Chunk results are cached (cache: true). If you change the simulator or its seed, render once with quarto render --cache-refresh so that cached chunks are rebuilt.


The simulator builds portfolios of twelve true types, spins each into one to four share classes, lets styles drift, blanks out some codes, and plants the data problems we will filter later. It is long, but the point of the lecture is what happens after it; skim it.


Code
simulate_crsp <- function(n_port = 1500, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # --- vendor style codes for broad domestic-equity funds (illustrative) ------
  broad <- tribble(
    ~lipper_obj_cd, ~lipper_class, ~si_obj_cd, ~wbrger_obj_cd, ~crsp_obj_cd,
    "G",  "LCGE", "GRO", "G",   "EDYG",
    "GI", "LCCE", "GRI", "GCI", "EDYB",
    "EI", "EIEI", "ING", "IEQ", "EDYI",
    "MC", "MCGE", "GMC", "MCG", "EDCM",
    "SG", "SCGE", "SCG", "SCG", "EDCS",
    "CA", "MLGE", "AGG", "LTG", "EDYG",
    "MR", "MLCE", "GRO", "IEQ", "EDCM"
  ) |> mutate(sid = row_number())

  sector <- tribble(
    ~lipper_obj_cd, ~lipper_class, ~si_obj_cd, ~wbrger_obj_cd, ~crsp_obj_cd, ~sector_name,
    "TK", "SPTK", "SEC", "S", "EDSF", "Technology",
    "H",  "SPHE", "SEC", "S", "EDSH", "Health Sciences",
    "FS", "SPFS", "SEC", "S", "EDSN", "Financial Services",
    "RE", "SPRE", "SEC", "S", "EDSR", "Real Estate",
    "UT", "SPUT", "SEC", "S", "EDSU", "Wind Energy"
  ) |> mutate(sid = row_number()) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_s"), -sid)

  type_lvls <- c("active_broad", "active_sector", "active_special",
                 "active_foreign_name", "index", "etf_index", "etf_active",
                 "etn", "enhanced", "target", "intl", "bond")
  type_prob <- c(.38, .07, .03, .02, .09, .05, .02, .01, .02, .06, .13, .12)

  families <- c("Alder", "Beacon", "Cedar", "Delta", "Everest",
                "Falcon", "Granite", "Harbor", "Juniper", "Kestrel")

  style_path <- function(n, k, p_switch = 0.04) {
    s <- integer(n); s[1] <- sample(k, 1)
    for (i in seq_len(n)[-1]) s[i] <- if (runif(1) < p_switch) sample(k, 1) else s[i - 1]
    s
  }

  # --- portfolios -------------------------------------------------------------
  port <- tibble(
    wficn     = 1:n_port,
    true_type = sample(type_lvls, n_port, TRUE, type_prob),
    family    = sample(families, n_port, TRUE)
  ) |>
    mutate(
      first_year = map_int(true_type, \(t) {
        lo <- switch(t, etf_index = , etf_active = , etn = 2000L, index = 1990L, 1985L)
        sample(lo:2022L, 1, prob = (lo:2022L) - lo + 5)   # launches grow over time
      }),
      last_year    = pmin(2023L, first_year + 2L + rgeom(n(), 0.07)),
      no_codes     = runif(n()) < 0.03,                   # some funds never carry a style code
      special_kind = sample(1:3, n(), TRUE),
      tdf_eq_code  = runif(n()) < 0.40,
      idx_flagged  = runif(n()) < 0.70,
      base_tna     = exp(rnorm(n(), 4.5, 1.8)),            # $ millions
      offer_month  = sample(1:12, n(), TRUE),
      first_offer  = as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-15", first_year, offer_month)),
      name_pick    = sample(1:11, n(), TRUE),
      trap_pick    = runif(n())
    ) |>
    filter(last_year >= 2000L)

  # --- fund names (with a few planted traps) ------------------------------------
  act_words <- c("Growth", "Value Opportunities", "Capital Appreciation", "Mid Cap",
                 "Small Cap", "Equity Income", "Blue Chip", "Dividend Growth",
                 "Select", "Contrarian", "Core")
  port <- port |>
    mutate(
      base_name = case_when(
        true_type == "active_broad" ~ paste(family, act_words[name_pick], "Fund"),
        true_type == "active_special" ~ paste(family, c("Market Neutral", "Short Alpha", "Covered Call")[special_kind], "Fund"),
        true_type == "active_foreign_name" ~ paste(family, c("China", "India", "Japan", "Asia", "Europe")[name_pick %% 5 + 1], "Opportunities Fund"),
        true_type == "index" ~ paste(family, c("500 Index", "Total Market Index", "Small Cap Index", "Value Index", "Growth Index", "Extended Market Index", "Russell 1000 Index", "Mid Cap Index", "Large Cap Idx", "Equity Index", "Total Stock Indx")[name_pick], "Fund"),
        true_type == "etf_index" ~ paste(family, c("Core S&P 500 ETF", "Total Market ETF", "Small Cap ETF", "Large Cap ETF", "Dividend ETF")[name_pick %% 5 + 1]),
        true_type == "etf_active" ~ paste(family, c("Active Growth ETF", "Active Value ETF", "Dynamic Equity ETF")[name_pick %% 3 + 1]),
        true_type == "etn" ~ paste(family, "Leveraged Energy ETN"),
        true_type == "enhanced" ~ paste(family, c("Ultra Equity", "2x Large Cap", "Enhanced Equity", "Equity Plus")[name_pick %% 4 + 1], "Fund"),
        true_type == "target" ~ paste(family, "Retirement", seq(2010, 2060, 5)[name_pick], "Fund"),
        true_type == "intl" ~ paste(family, c("International", "Global", "Emerging Markets", "World")[name_pick %% 4 + 1], "Fund"),
        true_type == "bond" ~ paste(family, c("Core Bond", "High Yield", "Municipal Bond")[name_pick %% 3 + 1], "Fund"),
        TRUE ~ paste(family, "Fund")
      ),
      # traps: names that fool naive substring rules
      base_name = if_else(true_type == "active_broad" & trap_pick < 0.04, paste(family, "Growth Fund RSP"), base_name),
      base_name = if_else(true_type == "active_broad" & trap_pick > 0.97, paste(family, "Select 100 Opportunities Fund"), base_name)
    )

  # --- share classes ----------------------------------------------------------------
  cls <- port |>
    mutate(n_cls = sample(1:4, n(), TRUE, c(.35, .30, .20, .15))) |>
    uncount(n_cls, .id = "k") |>
    mutate(crsp_fundno = 10000L + row_number(),
           crsp_cl_grp = 500000L + wficn,
           crsp_portno = if_else(runif(n()) < .8, 8000L + wficn, NA_integer_),
           w_cls       = c(.50, .30, .15, .05)[k]) |>
    mutate(class_share = w_cls / sum(w_cls), .by = wficn) |>
    select(wficn, k, crsp_fundno, crsp_cl_grp, crsp_portno, class_share)

  # --- portfolio-year panel with style paths ------------------------------------------
  pp <- port |>
    mutate(year = map2(pmax(first_year, 2000L), last_year, \(a, b) a:b)) |>
    unnest(year) |>
    mutate(style_id = style_path(n(), 7L,
                                 if (first(true_type) %in% c("active_broad", "active_special", "active_foreign_name")) 0.04 else 0),
           .by = wficn) |>
    mutate(sid = style_id, sid_s = ((style_id - 1L) %% 5L) + 1L) |>
    left_join(broad,  by = "sid") |>
    left_join(sector, by = c("sid_s" = "sid"))

  pp <- pp |>
    mutate(
      equity_coded = true_type %in% c("active_broad", "active_special", "active_foreign_name",
                                      "index", "etf_index", "etf_active", "etn", "enhanced") |
                     (true_type == "target" & tdf_eq_code),
      lipper_obj_cd = case_when(true_type == "active_sector" ~ lipper_obj_cd_s,
                                equity_coded ~ lipper_obj_cd,
                                true_type == "intl" ~ "IL", true_type == "bond" ~ "A",
                                TRUE ~ "MTD"),
      lipper_class  = case_when(true_type == "active_sector" ~ lipper_class_s,
                                equity_coded ~ lipper_class, TRUE ~ "OTHR"),
      si_obj_cd     = case_when(true_type == "active_sector" ~ si_obj_cd_s,
                                true_type == "active_special" & special_kind == 3L ~ "OPI",
                                equity_coded ~ si_obj_cd, TRUE ~ "OTH"),
      wbrger_obj_cd = case_when(true_type == "active_sector" ~ wbrger_obj_cd_s,
                                equity_coded ~ wbrger_obj_cd, TRUE ~ "OTH"),
      crsp_obj_cd   = case_when(true_type == "active_sector" ~ crsp_obj_cd_s,
                                true_type == "active_special" ~ c("EDYH", "EDYS", "EDYI")[special_kind],
                                equity_coded ~ crsp_obj_cd,
                                true_type == "intl" ~ "EICE", true_type == "bond" ~ "ICQY",
                                TRUE ~ "MTAL"),
      base_name = if_else(true_type == "active_sector",
                          paste(family, sector_name_s, "Fund"), base_name),
      age_y     = year - first_year,
      index_fund_flag = case_when(
        year < 2008 ~ NA_character_,
        true_type == "index" & idx_flagged ~ sample(c("D", "B"), n(), TRUE),
        true_type == "etf_index" ~ "D",
        true_type == "enhanced" ~ "E",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_),
      et_flag = case_when(true_type %in% c("etf_index", "etf_active") ~ "F",
                          true_type == "etn" ~ "N", TRUE ~ NA_character_),
      tna_port  = base_tna * exp(0.08 * pmin(pmax(age_y, 0), 20) + rnorm(n(), 0, .25))
    )

  blank <- function(x, p) if_else(runif(length(x)) < p, "", x)

  pp |>
    inner_join(cls, by = "wficn", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    mutate(
      class_suffix = c("A", "C", "I", "Admiral")[k],
      fund_name    = paste0(base_name, ";", class_suffix),
      caldt        = as.Date(sprintf("%d-12-31", year)),
      first_offer_dt = first_offer + (k - 1L) * 180L,
      tna_latest   = if_else(runif(n()) < 0.02, NA_real_, tna_port * class_share),
      er_mean      = case_when(str_detect(true_type, "^active") ~ .0115,
                               true_type == "index" ~ .0020,
                               str_detect(true_type, "^etf") ~ .0040, TRUE ~ .0100),
      exp_ratio    = pmax(.0005, rnorm(n(), er_mean, er_mean / 3) + c(0, .0075, 0, -.003)[k]),
      exp_ratio    = case_when(runif(n()) < .02  ~ -99,
                               runif(n()) < .005 ~ .15,
                               runif(n()) < .01  ~ NA_real_, TRUE ~ exp_ratio),
      across(c(lipper_obj_cd, crsp_obj_cd), \(x) blank(x, .06)),
      across(c(lipper_class, si_obj_cd, wbrger_obj_cd), \(x) blank(x, .25)),
      across(c(lipper_obj_cd, lipper_class, si_obj_cd, wbrger_obj_cd, crsp_obj_cd),
             \(x) if_else(no_codes, "", x))
    ) |>
    select(crsp_fundno, crsp_cl_grp, crsp_portno, wficn, fund_name, year, caldt,
           first_offer_dt, tna_latest, exp_ratio, lipper_class, lipper_obj_cd,
           si_obj_cd, wbrger_obj_cd, crsp_obj_cd, index_fund_flag, et_flag, true_type)
}




Code
fund_raw <- simulate_crsp(n_port = 1500, seed = 2026)

fund_raw <- fund_raw |> filter(!is.na(tna_latest))   # require non-missing TNA

cat("Data source: simulated CRSP-style panel", "\n",
    "Share-class-years:", format(nrow(fund_raw), big.mark = ","), "\n",
    "Share classes:    ", format(n_distinct(fund_raw$crsp_fundno), big.mark = ","), "\n",
    "Funds (WFICN):    ", format(n_distinct(fund_raw$wficn), big.mark = ","), "\n")

title: Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
section: 2. The Unit of Observation: Share Class vs. Fund
text:
2. The Unit of Observation: Share Class vs. Fund
A “fund” in CRSP is not one row. Most funds sell several share classes (A, C, institutional, …) that hold the same portfolio and differ only in fees and target clients. CRSP gives each share class its own identifier, and a handful of other identifiers sit above it.

CRSP fund identifiers







Identifier
Level
Use




crsp_fundno
Share class
Fees, loads, 12b-1 fees, and TNA differ by share class


crsp_cl_grp
Class group
CRSP’s grouping of share classes of the same fund


crsp_portno
Portfolio
Links to holdings; not populated for every share class


wficn
Fund
MFLINKS identifier that links CRSP to Thomson Reuters holdings



If we treat each share class as a fund, a fund with four share classes counts four times in every cross-section, and its alpha is counted four times in a skill test. The standard fix, used by Doshi et al. (2015), Back et al. (2018), and Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026), is to aggregate share classes to the portfolio level: TNA is summed, fund age is the age of the oldest share class, and all other characteristics (expense ratio, turnover) are TNA-weighted averages.


Code
toy <- tribble(
  ~class, ~first_offer_dt,  ~tna,  ~exp_ratio,
  "A",    "2004-03-15",     600,   0.0115,
  "C",    "2006-09-15",     150,   0.0190,
  "I",    "2009-01-15",     250,   0.0085
) |> mutate(first_offer_dt = as.Date(first_offer_dt))

toy_fund <- toy |>
  summarise(
    total_tna        = sum(tna),
    fund_first_offer = min(first_offer_dt),                 # oldest share class
    er_tna_weighted  = weighted.mean(exp_ratio, tna),
    er_simple_mean   = mean(exp_ratio)
  )

toy_fund |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = total_tna, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(er_tna_weighted, er_simple_mean), decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(total_tna = "Fund TNA ($M)", fund_first_offer = "Fund first offer date",
             er_tna_weighted = "Expense ratio (TNA-weighted)",
             er_simple_mean = "Expense ratio (simple mean)") |>
  tab_header(title = "Aggregating Three Share Classes into One Fund",
             subtitle = "The simple mean overstates the fee that the average dollar pays")








Aggregating Three Share Classes into One Fund


The simple mean overstates the fee that the average dollar pays


Fund TNA ($M)
Fund first offer date
Expense ratio (TNA-weighted)
Expense ratio (simple mean)

0.0130







The simple mean over-weights the expensive, small share class. The TNA-weighted average is what the average dollar invested in the fund actually pays.

title: Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
section: 3. Why Filter? Cleaning the CRSP Sample
text:
3. Why Filter? Cleaning the CRSP Sample
A raw CRSP extract is not a sample of “equity mutual funds”. It also contains bond funds, international funds, target-date funds, tiny funds, funds in their private incubation period, and funds with missing or nonsensical fields. Each of the papers below applies a short list of filters before computing anything. The filters look like housekeeping, but each one removes a specific, documented bias.

3.1 The Filters and Why They Exist

Sample filters used in the three papers







Filter
Rule (paper)
Why




Incubation / backfill
Drop the first 18 months of returns (Doshi et al. 2015); only use returns after the first offer date and when the fund name is non-missing (Back et al. 2018); drop the first 3 years of a fund’s life (Dannhauser and Pontiff 2026)
Funds incubated privately are opened to the public only after good results (Evans 2010)


Small funds
Drop fund-periods with TNA below $15 million (Doshi et al. 2015; Back et al. 2018; Dannhauser and Pontiff 2026)
Returns of very small funds are noisy and, as Elton et al. (2001) show, biased upward in CRSP


Equity share
Drop funds that on average hold less than 80% of assets in equity Kacperczyk et al. (2008)
Objective codes do not always describe what the fund really holds


Too few holdings
Drop observations with ten or fewer stock holdings (Doshi et al. 2015; Back et al. 2018)
Holdings-based measures become meaningless


Missing name
Drop funds with missing names (Doshi et al. 2015)
Names are needed for classification; missing names also flag backfilled periods (Back et al. 2018)


Missing fields
Drop observations with missing returns or expense ratio (Dannhauser and Pontiff 2026); require at least 60 days of returns and at least 90% non-missing daily returns (Back et al. 2018)
Reporting irregularities (for example weekly-reporting funds)


Not domestic equity
Keep CRSP objective codes starting with ED or the listed Lipper codes; drop China, Brazil, India, Europe, Asia, or Japan in the name (Dannhauser and Pontiff 2026)
Different asset class or mandate


Special products
Drop target-date funds (Parker et al. 2023), ETNs, leveraged and inverse funds, funds of funds, and active ETFs (Dannhauser and Pontiff 2026)
Different mandate; not comparable with plain-vanilla funds


Consistency
Require a fund to meet its type definition in at least 50% of its observations (Dannhauser and Pontiff 2026)
Avoids funds flagged as index for just 2% of their history



Three of these filters need data beyond the fund summary table: the 80% equity-share rule and the ten-holdings rule need holdings data (Thomson Reuters S12 or N-PORT), and the daily-return rules need the daily returns file. The pipeline in §3.3 implements the filters that can be applied to the summary table.


3.2 Incubation Bias: A Simulation
Evans (2010) documents the mechanism. A fund family starts several funds privately, often funded by the family itself, and tracks their results. After an evaluation period it opens only some of them to the public. The funds that are opened are, by construction, the ones that did well. Evans finds that incubated funds outperform non-incubated funds by roughly 3.5% on a risk-adjusted basis, that the outperformance disappears after the fund goes public, and that this inflates reported returns. A fund-size filter does not remove the bias, but fund-age and ticker-creation-date filters do.
We simulate the mechanism with zero skill: every fund’s true alpha is exactly zero.


Code
set.seed(2026)
n_fam <- 200; k <- 8                # 200 families, each incubates 8 private funds
T_inc <- 36; T_pub <- 60            # 36 private months, then 60 public months
sd_m  <- 0.018                      # monthly idiosyncratic volatility
release_share <- 0.25               # the best quarter of incubated funds are opened

# Incubated funds: monthly abnormal returns, true alpha = 0
inc <- expand_grid(family = 1:n_fam, fund = 1:k, age = 1:(T_inc + T_pub)) |>
  mutate(fid = paste(family, fund, sep = "-"),
         ar  = rnorm(n(), 0, sd_m))

# The family opens the funds with the best incubation record
released <- inc |>
  filter(age <= T_inc) |>
  summarise(cum_inc = sum(ar), .by = c(family, fund, fid)) |>
  mutate(rk = rank(-cum_inc), .by = family) |>
  filter(rk <= ceiling(release_share * k)) |>
  pull(fid)

inc_rel <- inc |> filter(fid %in% released) |> mutate(group = "Incubated, then opened")

# Comparison funds: never incubated, listed from their first month
n_ctrl <- 3 * length(released)
ctrl <- expand_grid(fund = 1:n_ctrl, age = 1:(T_inc + T_pub)) |>
  mutate(fid = paste0("c", fund), ar = rnorm(n(), 0, sd_m), group = "Not incubated")

sim_funds <- bind_rows(inc_rel, ctrl) |> select(group, fid, age, ar)

cat("Incubated funds opened:", length(released), "of", n_fam * k, "\n",
    "Never-incubated funds: ", n_ctrl, "\n")


Incubated funds opened: 400 of 1600 
 Never-incubated funds:  1200 




Code
cum_path <- sim_funds |>
  arrange(group, fid, age) |>
  mutate(cum_ar = cumsum(ar), .by = c(group, fid)) |>
  summarise(mean_cum = mean(cum_ar) * 100, .by = c(group, age))

hchart(cum_path, "line", hcaes(x = age, y = mean_cum, group = group)) |>
  hc_chart(zoomType = "x", height = 420) |>
  hc_title(text = "True alpha is zero for every fund") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = "Fund age (months)"),
           plotLines = list(list(value = T_inc, color = "#444444", width = 1,
                                 dashStyle = "Dash", zIndex = 3,
                                 label = list(text = "Fund opens to the public",
                                              rotation = 0, y = 12, x = 6)))) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Mean cumulative abnormal return (%)"),
           labels = list(format = "{value}%")) |>
  hc_tooltip(shared = TRUE, valueDecimals = 2, valueSuffix = "%") |>
  hc_plotOptions(series = list(lineWidth = 2, marker = list(enabled = FALSE)))








Figure 1: Average cumulative abnormal return by fund age: incubated funds look skilled only while they are private




The released funds climb steadily while private, because the family selected them on that very record. Once the fund is open, the line goes flat: the selection effect is gone, and the true alpha of zero is visible. The never-incubated funds are flat throughout.
Why this matters: if the database backfills the private record into the fund’s history and we use it, a pooled estimate is biased upward and “skilled” managers appear. We can measure both effects in the simulation.


Code
eval_sample <- function(d, label) {
  fund_stats <- d |>
    summarise(m = mean(ar), s = sd(ar), n = n(), .by = c(group, fid)) |>
    mutate(t = m / (s / sqrt(n)))
  inc_only <- d$group == "Incubated, then opened"
  tibble(sample = label,
         `Pooled alpha (% per year)`          = mean(d$ar) * 1200,
         `Incubated funds only (% per year)`  = mean(d$ar[inc_only]) * 1200,
         `Funds with t > 1.96 (%)`            = mean(fund_stats$t > 1.96) * 100,
         `... incubated funds only (%)`       = mean(fund_stats$t[fund_stats$group == "Incubated, then opened"] > 1.96) * 100)
}

bind_rows(
  eval_sample(sim_funds, "No filter (backfilled history included)"),
  eval_sample(filter(sim_funds, age > T_inc), "Drop first 36 months of every fund")
) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = 2:5, decimals = 2) |>
  tab_header(title = "Same Funds, Same Returns, Different Conclusions",
             subtitle = "True alpha = 0 for every fund; a one-sided 5% test should flag about 2.5% by luck") |>
  tab_source_note("Illustrative simulation; parameters are chosen for visibility, not calibrated to CRSP.")




Table 1: Incubation bias: pooled alpha and false ‘skilled’ funds, before and after the age filter









Same Funds, Same Returns, Different Conclusions


True alpha = 0 for every fund; a one-sided 5% test should flag about 2.5% by luck


sample

Incubated funds only (% per year)
Funds with t > 1.96 (%)
... incubated funds only (%)




No filter (backfilled history included)
