Illustrative simulation; parameters are chosen for visibility, not calibrated to CRSP.











Without the filter, the incubated funds show a sizeable positive alpha and several times the luck rate of statistically “skilled” funds, even though every fund has zero true alpha. The pooled alpha is smaller because only a quarter of the simulated funds were incubated, but it is still visibly positive. With the age filter, both alphas fall to roughly zero and the share of “skilled” funds returns to the luck rate. (The remaining differences from exactly zero are sampling noise.) This connects directly to Lecture 2: incubation bias is a selection problem, so it feeds the false discoveries that the luck-versus-skill tests are designed to count.






Important



Three papers, three versions of the same fix. Doshi et al. (2015) drop 18 months, Back et al. (2018) use the first offer date and the name-availability date, and Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) drop three years (which also removes the burst of newly launched ETFs that cater to investor sentiment, see Ben-David et al. (2023)). The longer the window, the safer the filter, and the more young funds you lose. This is a design choice that you should report and test for robustness.




3.3 The Filter Pipeline, Step by Step
We now apply the filters that can be applied to the fund summary table and record how many funds survive each step. First, the helpers and the classification flags used in the pipeline (they are explained in §4).


Code
blank_to_na <- function(x) if_else(x == "", NA_character_, x)
mode_chr    <- function(x) {                        # most frequent non-missing value
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x) == 0) return(NA_character_)
  names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
}

# ---- Dannhauser & Pontiff (2026) parameters ---------------------------------
dp_lipper  <- c("CA", "EI", "G", "GI", "MC", "MR", "SG", "SP", "BM", "CG", "CS",
                "FS", "H", "ID", "N", "RE", "TK", "TL", "S", "UT")
dp_foreign <- "china|brazil|india|europe|asia|japan"
dp_index_names <- paste0("index|idx|indx|ind |composite|russell|s&p|s and p|s & p|",
                         "msci|bloomberg|kbw|nasdaq|nyse|stoxx|ftse|wilshire|",
                         "morningstar|100|400|500|600|900|1000|1500|2000|3000|5000")
dp_etf_names   <- "etf|ishares|spdr|holdrs|streettracks|exchange traded|exchange-traded"
dp_enh_names   <- "plus|enhanced|inverse|bull|bear|2x|3x|ultra|1\\.5x|2\\.5x"

# ---- Target-date funds (Parker, Schoar, and Sun 2023): name contains a vintage
identify_tdf <- function(x, year) {
  # a year, but not when it follows "Russell" or "Russ" (the Russell 2000 index)
  td <- if_else(str_detect(x, sprintf("(?<!Russell ?|Russ ?)%i", year)), 1, 0)
  td <- if_else(str_detect(x, sprintf("%i\\+|V%i|AXA Tactical|AXA %i|%i ETF|Focused %i Value",
                                      year, year, year, year, year)), 1, td)
  td
}

flag_types <- function(d) {
  d |>
    mutate(
      name_lc = str_to_lower(coalesce(fund_name, "")),

      # Step 1 of DP (2026): domestic-equity universe
      domestic_equity =
        (coalesce(str_starts(crsp_obj_cd, "ED"), FALSE) | lipper_obj_cd %in% dp_lipper) &
        !str_detect(name_lc, dp_foreign),

      # Passive funds: CRSP index flag D or B, or a name match
      index_fund = coalesce(index_fund_flag %in% c("D", "B"), FALSE) |
                   str_detect(coalesce(fund_name, ""), "SP|DOW|Dow|DJ") |
                   str_detect(name_lc, dp_index_names),

      # Exchange-traded products
      ETF = coalesce(et_flag == "F", FALSE) | str_detect(name_lc, dp_etf_names),
      ETN = coalesce(et_flag == "N", FALSE) | str_detect(coalesce(fund_name, ""), "ETN") |
            str_detect(name_lc, "exchange traded note|exchange-traded note"),

      # Leveraged / inverse / enhanced
      enhanced = coalesce(index_fund_flag == "E", FALSE) | str_detect(name_lc, dp_enh_names),

      # Target-date funds
      target = reduce(map(seq(2000, 2065, by = 5), \(y) identify_tdf(coalesce(fund_name, ""), y)),
                      `|`) == 1
    )
}




Code
steps <- list()
log_step <- function(label, d, unit) {
  steps[[length(steps) + 1]] <<- tibble(step = label, unit = unit,
                                        n_obs = nrow(d), n_funds = n_distinct(d$wficn))
}

style_cols <- c("lipper_class", "lipper_obj_cd", "si_obj_cd", "wbrger_obj_cd", "crsp_obj_cd")

# 0. Raw
d <- fund_raw
log_step("0. Raw file (2000+, year-end, TNA non-missing)", d, "share-class-years")

# 1. Style codes: drop funds that never have a Lipper or CRSP objective code
d <- d |>
  mutate(across(all_of(style_cols), blank_to_na)) |>
  mutate(no_style = all(is.na(lipper_obj_cd) & is.na(crsp_obj_cd)), .by = crsp_fundno) |>
  filter(!no_style) |>
  select(-no_style)
log_step("1. Drop funds with no style code in any year", d, "share-class-years")

# 2. Fill missing style codes: carry the last known code forward, then back-fill the start
d <- d |>
  arrange(crsp_fundno, year) |>
  group_by(crsp_fundno) |>
  fill(all_of(style_cols), .direction = "downup") |>
  ungroup()

# 3. Flag types, then remove ETNs, leveraged/inverse funds, and target-date funds
d <- flag_types(d)
d <- d |> filter(!(ETN | enhanced | target))
log_step("2. Drop ETNs, leveraged/inverse, target-date funds", d, "share-class-years")

# 4. Domestic equity for at least 50% of a fund's observations, then keep those years
d <- d |>
  mutate(share_dom = mean(domestic_equity), .by = crsp_fundno) |>
  filter(share_dom >= 0.5, domestic_equity)
log_step("3. Domestic equity (CRSP/Lipper codes; no foreign names; >= 50% of years)", d, "share-class-years")

# 5. Drop active ETFs (ETF flag but not passive); label the three vehicle types
d <- d |>
  filter(!(ETF & !index_fund)) |>
  mutate(fund_type = case_when(ETF ~ "ETF", index_fund ~ "Index", TRUE ~ "Active"))
log_step("4. Drop active ETFs; label Active / Index / ETF", d, "share-class-years")

# 6. Aggregate share classes to the fund (WFICN) level
d <- d |>
  mutate(exp_ratio_clean = if_else(exp_ratio == -99 | exp_ratio > 0.1, NA_real_, exp_ratio)) |>
  mutate(fund_first_offer = min(first_offer_dt, na.rm = TRUE), .by = wficn)   # oldest share class

fund_year <- d |>
  summarise(
    fund_type      = mode_chr(fund_type),
    lipper_obj_cd  = mode_chr(lipper_obj_cd),
    true_type      = mode_chr(true_type),
    total_tna      = sum(tna_latest, na.rm = TRUE),
    exp_ratio      = weighted.mean(exp_ratio_clean, tna_latest, na.rm = TRUE),
    first_offer_dt = first(fund_first_offer),
    caldt          = max(caldt),
    n_classes      = n(),
    .by = c(wficn, year)
  ) |>
  mutate(fund_age = time_length(caldt - first_offer_dt, unit = "year"))
log_step("5. Aggregate share classes to funds (WFICN-years)", fund_year, "fund-years")

# 7. Incubation: drop the first three years of a fund's life (DP 2026)
fund_year <- fund_year |> filter(fund_age >= 3)
log_step("6. Drop first 3 years of life (incubation bias)", fund_year, "fund-years")

# 8. Size: drop fund-years with TNA below $15 million
fund_year <- fund_year |> filter(total_tna >= 15)
log_step("7. Drop TNA below $15 million", fund_year, "fund-years")

# 9. Missing or invalid expense ratio (DP 2026)
fund_year <- fund_year |> filter(!is.na(exp_ratio), is.finite(exp_ratio))
log_step("8. Drop missing / invalid expense ratio", fund_year, "fund-years")

attrition <- bind_rows(steps)




Code
attrition |>
  mutate(pct_funds = n_funds / first(n_funds)) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(n_obs, n_funds), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = pct_funds, decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(step = "Step", unit = "Unit", n_obs = "Observations",
             n_funds = "Funds (WFICN)", pct_funds = "% of raw funds") |>
  tab_header(title = "How Many Funds Survive Each Filter?",
             subtitle = "Simulated CRSP-style panel")

text:
4. Classifying Funds: Active, Index, or ETF?

4.1 Why Classification Is Not a Detail
The industry the literature studied in the 1990s is not the industry today. Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) report that active funds held more than 82% of domestic-equity fund assets at the start of their 2005–2022 sample and 43% at the end, while index mutual funds rose from 11% to 24% and ETFs from 7% to 33%. Studying “equity funds” now means studying three vehicles at once, and any test that pools them without labels mixes mandates. Their central finding about flows (performance chasing is pervasive in all three vehicles, with ETFs the most sensitive) can only be seen because the three vehicles are separated first.
The label also matters for skill evaluation. A closet indexer or an index fund has near-zero alpha by construction, so pooling it into a luck-versus-skill test (Lecture 2) dilutes the tails.


4.2 Three Recipes
All three papers start from the same raw data (CRSP objective codes and fund names) but define “an active domestic equity fund” differently.

Three classification recipes









Doshi et al. (2015)
Back et al. (2018)
Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026)




Core rule
A fund counts if any of four vendor codes (Lipper class, Lipper objective, Strategic Insight, Wiesenberger) is on a list of diversified-equity styles
CRSP objective code has E in the first position, D in the second, and C or Y in the third
CRSP objective code starts with ED or Lipper objective code is on a list that includes sector styles


Exclusions
International, balanced, sector, bond, money market, and index funds (by style and name)
Hedged or short funds (YH / YS), option-income funds (si_obj_cd = OPI), index and target-date funds
Names containing China, Brazil, India, Europe, Asia, Japan; ETNs, leveraged/inverse funds, funds of funds, active ETFs, target-date funds


Passive funds
Dropped
Dropped
Kept and labeled (CRSP index flag D/B, or index-related name strings)


ETFs
Not in sample
Not in sample
Kept and labeled (CRSP ETF identifier or name)


Consistency


Must satisfy the definition in at least 50% of observations


Goal
Sample of diversified, actively managed funds for an activeness study
Sample of active funds for a coskewness study
A comprehensive, comparable sample of all domestic-equity vehicles



Doshi et al. (2015) note in a footnote that a sample defined with the CRSP objective code is nearly identical to the one obtained with the Lipper, Strategic Insight, and Wiesenberger codes, so the first two recipes should agree closely. Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) differ because their goal is not a clean active sample. They want all domestic-equity vehicles (broad-based and sector), then separate passive from active.


4.3 Implementation and Comparison
We implement the three rules as functions that return a TRUE/FALSE flag per share-class-year, and apply them to the same data (after style-code filling, so they see the same codes).


Code
# Method 1: Doshi, Elkamhi, and Simutin (2015) -- union of vendor style codes
doshi_flag <- function(d) {
  vendor <- (d$lipper_class %in% c("EIEI", "G", "LCCE", "LCGE", "LCVE", "MCCE", "MCGE",
                                   "MCVE", "MLCE", "MLGE", "MLVE", "SCCE", "SCGE", "SCVE")) |
            (d$lipper_obj_cd %in% c("CA", "EI", "G", "GI", "MC", "MR", "SG")) |
            (d$si_obj_cd     %in% c("AGG", "GMC", "GRI", "GRO", "ING", "SCG")) |
            (d$wbrger_obj_cd %in% c("G", "GCI", "IEQ", "LTG", "MCG", "SCG"))
  vendor & !(d$index_fund_flag %in% c("B", "D", "E")) &
    !str_detect(str_to_lower(coalesce(d$fund_name, "")), "index|international|global|bond|balanced")
}

# Method 2: Back, Crane, and Crotty (2018) -- CRSP objective code ED(C|Y), no hedged/short/option income
back_flag <- function(d) {
  is_tdf <- reduce(map(seq(2000, 2065, by = 5),
                       \(y) identify_tdf(coalesce(d$fund_name, ""), y)), `|`) == 1
  coalesce(str_detect(d$crsp_obj_cd, "^ED[CY]"), FALSE) &
    !coalesce(str_detect(d$crsp_obj_cd, "^ED(YH|YS)"), FALSE) &
    (is.na(d$si_obj_cd) | d$si_obj_cd != "OPI") &
    !(d$index_fund_flag %in% c("B", "D", "E")) &      # index funds out (by CRSP flag)
    !is_tdf                                           # target-date funds out
}

# Method 3: Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) -- domestic-equity universe, then passive vs. active
dp_flag <- function(d) {
  dd <- flag_types(d)
  dd$domestic_equity & !dd$index_fund & !dd$ETF & !dd$ETN & !dd$enhanced & !dd$target
}

cmp_raw <- fund_raw |>
  mutate(across(all_of(style_cols), blank_to_na)) |>
  arrange(crsp_fundno, year) |>
  group_by(crsp_fundno) |>
  fill(all_of(style_cols), .direction = "downup") |>
  ungroup()

cmp <- cmp_raw |>
  mutate(m_doshi = doshi_flag(cmp_raw),
         m_back  = back_flag(cmp_raw),
         m_dp    = dp_flag(cmp_raw))

by_fund <- cmp |>
  summarise(across(c(m_doshi, m_back, m_dp), any), true_type = mode_chr(true_type),
            .by = wficn)

Because the data are simulated, we know the truth. The chart below shows which true fund types each recipe lets in.


Code
truth_lbl <- c(active_broad = "Active, broad", active_sector = "Active, sector",
               active_special = "Hedged / short / option income",
               active_foreign_name = "Domestic code, foreign name",
               index = "Index fund", etf_index = "Index ETF", etf_active = "Active ETF",
               etn = "ETN", enhanced = "Leveraged / enhanced", target = "Target-date",
               intl = "International", bond = "Bond")

truth_df <- by_fund |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("m_"), names_to = "method", values_to = "flag") |>
  filter(flag) |>
  count(method, true_type) |>
  mutate(method = recode(method, m_doshi = "Doshi et al.", m_back = "Back et al.",
                         m_dp = "Dannhauser & Pontiff"),
         true_type = factor(unname(truth_lbl[true_type]), levels = unname(truth_lbl))) |>
  complete(method, true_type, fill = list(n = 0))

hchart(truth_df, "column", hcaes(x = method, y = n, group = true_type)) |>
  hc_chart(height = 450) |>
  hc_title(text = "Composition of each recipe's 'active equity' sample") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL)) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Funds flagged (WFICN)"), reversedStacks = FALSE) |>
  hc_plotOptions(column = list(stacking = "normal")) |>
  hc_tooltip(shared = FALSE, pointFormat = "{series.name}: <b>{point.y}</b>")








Figure 3: What each recipe lets in, by true fund type




The pattern is the lesson. The vendor-code recipe and the CRSP-code recipe return mostly broad active funds, and the differences between them sit at the edges: Doshi’s vendor codes keep the hedged, short, and option-income funds and some target-date funds that Back’s CRSP-code rule drops, while Back’s rule, which removes index funds only through the CRSP index flag, lets in index funds whose flag is missing (in this panel the flag starts in 2008, mimicking its late start in CRSP). Both let in funds with a domestic code but a foreign name. The Dannhauser-Pontiff recipe adds the sector funds (which is intentional) and strips out passive products and ETFs by design. Choosing a recipe is choosing a population, and the population determines the answer.


4.4 Classification by Name: Powerful, and Easy to Get Wrong
Index funds, ETFs, ETNs, leveraged funds, and target-date funds are found partly by searching fund names. Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) hand-validate their name parsing, and they point out false positives, including a Mairs & Power fund that was wrongly identified as an index fund (their fn. 12). Substring rules fire in unexpected places. We test the rules on a small set of fictional names.


Code
trap <- tribble(
  ~fund_name,                              ~truth,
  "Vanguard-like 500 Index Fund",           "index fund",
  "Alder Total Stock Indx Fund",            "index fund",
  "Granite Growth Fund RSP",                "active fund",
  "Alder Wind Energy Fund",                 "active fund",
  "Beacon Select 100 Opportunities Fund",   "active fund",
  "Cedar Retirement 2040 Fund",             "target-date fund",
  "Delta Russell 2000 Alpha Fund",          "active fund",
  "Falcon Core S&P 500 ETF",                "index ETF",
  "Harbor Ultra Equity Fund",               "leveraged fund",
  "Juniper Equity Plus Fund",               "enhanced fund",
  "Kestrel Surplus Value Fund",             "active fund"
)

trap_flags <- trap |>
  mutate(
    nm_lc = str_to_lower(fund_name),
    # DP substring rules, as published
    `index (substring)` = str_detect(fund_name, "SP|DOW|Dow|DJ") | str_detect(nm_lc, dp_index_names),
    # a stricter version: whole words only
    `index (whole words)` = str_detect(fund_name, "\\b(SP|DOW|Dow|DJ)\\b") |
      str_detect(nm_lc, "\\b(index|idx|indx|composite|russell|s&p|msci|nasdaq|nyse|ftse|wilshire)\\b"),
    enhanced = str_detect(nm_lc, dp_enh_names),
    `target-date` = reduce(map(seq(2000, 2065, 5), \(y) identify_tdf(fund_name, y)), `|`) == 1
  ) |>
  select(-nm_lc)

trap_flags |>
  gt() |>
  data_color(columns = c(`index (substring)`, `index (whole words)`, enhanced, `target-date`),
             fn = \(x) if_else(x, "#f4b6b6", "white")) |>

             subtitle = "Red = flagged. Check each red cell against the 'truth' column") |>
  tab_source_note("Fictional fund names. 'SP' occurs inside 'RSP'; 'ind ' occurs inside 'wind '; digits occur in many names; 'plus' occurs inside 'surplus'.")

4.5 Fund Types Over Time
With the labels in place, we can reproduce the kind of picture in Figure 1 of Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026): the industry’s shift from active funds to index funds and ETFs.


Code
type_year <- fund_year |>
  count(year, fund_type, name = "n") |>
  mutate(fund_type = factor(fund_type, levels = c("Active", "Index", "ETF")),
         year = as.character(year)) |>
  complete(year, fund_type, fill = list(n = 0))

hchart(type_year, "column", hcaes(x = year, y = n, group = fund_type)) |>

  summarise(tna = sum(total_tna), .by = c(year, fund_type)) |>
  mutate(share = tna / sum(tna) * 100, .by = year) |>
  mutate(fund_type = factor(fund_type, levels = c("Active", "Index", "ETF")),
         year = as.character(year)) |>

hchart(tna_year, "column", hcaes(x = year, y = share, group = fund_type)) |>

           labels = list(format = "{value}%")) |>

Figure 5: Share of total net assets by vehicle type, by year










Note



The published picture is the benchmark: Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) find the active-fund share of assets falling from above 82% to 43%, index funds rising from 11% to 24%, and ETFs from 7% to 33% over 2005–2022. The simulated panel is not calibrated to those numbers, so read the two charts above for the mechanics, not the levels. Run on a real CRSP extract, the same code is a replication of their Figure 1.




4.6 Beyond Active vs. Passive: The Four-Tier Style View
Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) add a second dimension, following Ben-David et al. (2023), which classifies each fund by what it tracks:

Four-tier classification (Ben-David et al. 2023; Dannhauser and Pontiff 2026)






Tier
Definition (Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026))




Broad-based
Well-diversified benchmark without a strategic tilt


Strategic (smart) beta
Replicates known factor exposures


Sector
Follows a specific economic sector or industry


Thematic
Concentrates on a small set of social, environmental, or other issues



They report that the industry’s mix across these tiers moved too: broad-based funds held 30.5% of industry assets at the start of the sample and 44.8% at the end, strategic-beta funds fell from 63.6% to 44.9%, sector funds rose from 5.5% to 9.4%, and thematic funds from 0.5% to 0.9%. They also note that most active mutual funds are classified as strategic beta.


Code
tiers <- tribble(
  ~tier,                        ~period,        ~share,
  "Broad-based",                "Start (2005)",  30.5,
  "Strategic beta",             "Start (2005)",  63.6,
  "Sector",                     "Start (2005)",   5.5,
  "Thematic",                   "Start (2005)",   0.5,
  "Broad-based",                "End (2022)",    44.8,
  "Strategic beta",             "End (2022)",    44.9,
  "Sector",                     "End (2022)",     9.4,
  "Thematic",                   "End (2022)",     0.9
) |>
  mutate(tier = factor(tier, levels = c("Broad-based", "Strategic beta", "Sector", "Thematic")),
         period = factor(period, levels = c("Start (2005)", "End (2022)")))

hchart(tiers, "column", hcaes(x = period, y = share, group = tier)) |>
  hc_chart(height = 380) |>
  hc_title(text = "Share of industry assets, by tier") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL)) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "% of industry assets"), max = 100,
           labels = list(format = "{value}%")) |>
  hc_plotOptions(column = list(stacking = "normal",
                               dataLabels = list(enabled = TRUE, format = "{y:.1f}%"))) |>
  hc_tooltip(pointFormat = "{series.name}: <b>{point.y:.1f}%</b>")








Figure 6: Industry assets by four-tier classification, start and end of the Dannhauser-Pontiff sample (values reported in the paper)




The tier is itself a style label, which brings us to the next topic.


4.7 Name-Based Thematic Flags: An ESG Example
The thematic tier is usually found by name. A common research use is an ESG fund flag built from a keyword list. A regex with a character class in place of a negation is a classic bug: [^inflation] means “any one character that is not i, n, f, l, a, t, or o”, not “anything except the word inflation”.


Code
esg_names <- tribble(
  ~fund_name,
  "Alder Social Awareness Fund",
  "Beacon Social Media Fund",
  "Cedar Social Impact Fund",
  "Delta Inflation Response Fund",
  "Everest Climate Response Fund",
  "Granite Climate Alert Response Fund",
  "Falcon Responsible Growth Fund"
) |> mutate(nm = str_to_lower(fund_name))

esg_names |>
  mutate(
    `class: social [^media]` = str_detect(nm, "social [^media]"),
    `lookahead: social (?!media)` = str_detect(nm, "social (?!media)"),
    `class: [^inflation] response` = str_detect(nm, "[^inflation] response"),
    `lookbehind: (?<!inflation) response` = str_detect(nm, "(?<!inflation) response")
  ) |>
  select(-nm) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Same Intent, Different Regex",
             subtitle = "The character-class versions miss 'Social Awareness' and 'Alert Response' (the letters a and t sit inside the excluded set)")

title: Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
text:
5. Fund Style

5.1 What Is a Style?
An investment style is a persistent tilt in what a fund holds: large vs. small stocks, growth vs. value, high-momentum vs. low-momentum. Investors use styles to build portfolios (a “core and satellite” mix of style funds), and researchers use them to choose benchmarks and to measure what a manager adds beyond a style bet. There are three ways to learn a fund’s style, and they can disagree.

Three ways to measure a fund’s style







Approach
Where the style comes from
Examples




Stated
The label the fund or a data vendor assigns: prospectus objective, Lipper or Morningstar category, CRSP objective code
CRSP vendor codes; Kim et al. (2000) on objective misclassification


Returns-based
Regress the fund’s returns on style-index returns, with or without constraints
Sharpe (1992) style analysis; Brown and Goetzmann (1997); Carhart loadings (Lecture 1)


Holdings-based
Characteristics of the stocks the fund actually holds (size, book-to-market, momentum)
Daniel et al. (1997); Chan et al. (2002); Morningstar’s style box



A fund’s stated style is cheap, available for the whole CRSP universe, and what investors and the media see. It is also what the fund chooses to say, so it can lag, or be chosen for marketing reasons. Cooper et al. (2005) show that funds that change their names to match a hot style attract inflows whether or not the holdings change. Revealed style is harder to compute but cannot be changed with a press release.


5.2 Stated Style in the CRSP Data
CRSP carries several vendor coding systems side by side. We used them all in Section 4, because the three classification recipes differ mainly in which of them they trust.


Code
tribble(
  ~Field,           ~Source,                 ~Granularity,                                    ~`Used by`,
  "lipper_class",   "Lipper",                "Fine (e.g., large-cap core, mid-cap value)",    "Doshi",
  "lipper_obj_cd",  "Lipper",                "Coarse (e.g., G, GI, EI, MC, SG)",              "Doshi, Dannhauser-Pontiff",
  "si_obj_cd",      "Strategic Insight",     "Coarse; flags 'option income' (OPI)",           "Doshi, Back",
  "wbrger_obj_cd",  "Wiesenberger",          "Coarse",                   "Doshi",
  "crsp_obj_cd",    "CRSP (own hierarchy)",  "ED... = domestic equity; 3rd-4th letter = style", "Back, Dannhauser-Pontiff"
) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Where a Stated Style Comes From",
             subtitle = "Vendors cover different periods and use different taxonomies")

A style label only matters if it is stable enough to mean something. Here is the composition of active domestic-equity funds by Lipper objective code in our cleaned sample. Codes outside the seven broad styles (sector, specialty) are pooled as “Other”.


Code
lipper_labels <- tribble(
  ~code, ~label,
  "CA", "Capital appreciation",
  "EI", "Equity income",
  "G",  "Growth",
  "GI", "Growth & income",
  "MC", "Mid-cap",
  "MR", "Multi-cap",
  "SG", "Small-cap"
)
# (Illustrative names; the CRSP data guide has the authoritative definitions.)

lump_style <- function(x) if_else(x %in% lipper_labels$code, x, "Other")

style_mix <- fund_year |>
  filter(fund_type == "Active", !is.na(lipper_obj_cd)) |>
  mutate(style = lump_style(lipper_obj_cd), year = as.character(year)) |>
  count(year, style) |>
  complete(year, style, fill = list(n = 0L))




Code

  hc_chart(height = 400) |>
  hc_title(text = "Active funds by stated style") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL)) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "% of active funds"), labels = list(format = "{value}%")) |>
  hc_plotOptions(column = list(stacking = "percent")) |>
  hc_tooltip(shared = TRUE, pointFormat = "{series.name}: <b>{point.percentage:.1f}%</b><br/>")








Figure 7: Share of active domestic-equity funds by Lipper objective code (stacked to 100%)






5.3 Why Style Matters for Empirical Work

Benchmarks. A fund’s alpha depends on the benchmark, and the right benchmark depends on the style (Lecture 1). A “growth” label with a value portfolio produces an alpha that is just a style bet.
Characteristic-adjusted performance. Daniel et al. (1997) benchmark each stock a fund holds against a portfolio matched on size, book-to-market, and momentum, so that style exposure is not mistaken for skill.
Flows and prices. Barberis and Shleifer (2003) model investors who allocate money across styles rather than individual stocks, so style-level flows move prices of stocks in the same style.
Selection into samples. Many studies pool “growth funds” or “small-cap funds”. If the label is wrong, the pooled estimate describes some other group of funds. Kim et al. (2000) document objective misclassification.
Fund-level controls. Style fixed effects absorb the performance differences that come from the fund’s mandate.







TipThe Morningstar style box



Holdings-based styles are often shown on a 3 x 3 grid. A fund’s portfolio is placed in one cell by the average size and value/growth characteristics of its holdings. Each cell has a name, and the box tells investors in a glance which part of the market a fund covers.




Value
Blend

Large growth


Mid

Small
Small value
Small blend
Small growth



A fund is assigned to a cell by the average characteristics of its holdings. A fund can sit on a cell boundary and move cells for small changes in its holdings, which is one way a measured style drift can arise without any decision by the manager.

title: Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
text:
6. Style Drift

6.1 What Is Style Drift?
Style drift is a change in a fund’s style over time. Two questions come up right away.
Why does the style change? There are two sources. In active drift, the manager changes the portfolio: from growth to value, from small to large, or chasing whatever has recently done well. In passive drift, the stocks migrate while the manager holds them: a small-cap fund’s winners grow into mid-caps, so the fund looks larger without a single trade. The two have different implications, and holdings data can separate them, because only active drift involves trading (Wermers 2012).
Which style do we measure? We can measure drift in the stated label (a change in the Lipper code) or in the revealed style (a change in estimated factor loadings or in the characteristics of the stocks held). The first is available for the whole universe and easy to compute. The second needs returns or holdings, and it works even when the label never changes. A fund that keeps its “growth” label while holding a value portfolio is a drifting fund that the label cannot detect.

Two ways to measure style drift








Stated drift
Revealed drift




Data
Vendor style code by year
Fund returns (loadings) or holdings (characteristics)


Frequency
Annual, whole CRSP universe
Monthly or quarterly, rolling or non-overlapping windows


Detects
Label changes (and coding noise)
Changes in actual exposure


Misses
Drift under a constant label
Short windows; estimation noise



Why would anyone care? An investor who combines a growth fund and a value fund for diversification relies on each fund to stay what it is. A researcher who benchmarks a fund by its style needs the style to hold over the evaluation window. And drift can be a symptom of incentives: a manager who is behind in the annual race has reasons to change strategy (Brown et al. 1996; Chevalier and Ellison 1997).
The rest of this section is organized around one paper. §6.2 reports what Chan et al. (2002) find, §6.3 rebuilds their design on simulated funds so that you can see what it can and cannot detect, and §6.4–§6.6 apply the same ideas to stated labels and to individual real funds.


6.2 The Key Paper: Chan, Chen, and Lakonishok (2002)
Chan et al. (2002) is the classic empirical study of mutual fund styles. It asks four questions: where do funds sit in the style space, how consistent are styles over time, which funds change style, and does performance differ across styles once style is accounted for.
Data. Morningstar monthly returns from 1976 to 1997 and portfolio holdings from 1983, for the 3,336 U.S. domestic equity funds in existence at the end of 1997. Morningstar’s data on defunct funds start only in 1989, so the early years carry survivorship bias, a point the authors acknowledge.
Two ways to measure style, which map onto the stated/revealed distinction above (both are revealed measures; the paper does not rely on vendor labels):

Characteristics (holdings-based). Every stock is ranked from 0 (lowest) to 1 (highest) on size, book-to-market, and past return. A fund’s score on each dimension is the holdings-weighted average of its stocks’ ranks.
Factor loadings (returns-based). The fund’s Fama-French three-factor loadings, estimated over the past 36 months, are ranked across funds from 0 to 1.

Measuring consistency. At each year-end from 1984 to 1994, a fund’s style rank is computed from the past three years and again from the following, non-overlapping three years. Consistency is the cross-sectional correlation between the past and future ranks, together with the average absolute change in rank. Non-overlapping windows matter: with overlapping windows, the two ranks would share data and look consistent by construction.
Measuring who drifts. Funds are sorted two ways: by past two-year return (winners are the top 20%, losers the bottom 20%) and by style (top, middle, and bottom 30%). The average absolute change in style rank is then compared across the cells.

What they find

The second is the paper’s central drift result: style changes are concentrated among funds that performed poorly, and specifically among value funds that performed poorly.

ccl_t8 <- tribble(
  ~group,         ~winners, ~losers,
  "All funds",       0.077,   0.100,
  "Value funds",     0.060,   0.120
)

highchart() |>
  hc_chart(type = "column", height = 360) |>
  hc_title(text = "Losers drift, especially losing value funds") |>
  hc_xAxis(categories = ccl_t8$group) |>
  hc_add_series(name = "Past winners (top 20%)",  data = ccl_t8$winners) |>
  hc_add_series(name = "Past losers (bottom 20%)", data = ccl_t8$losers) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Mean |change in B/M rank|"), min = 0) |>
  hc_plotOptions(column = list(dataLabels = list(enabled = TRUE, format = "{y:.3f}"))) |>
  hc_tooltip(shared = TRUE, valueDecimals = 3)








Figure 9: Average absolute change in book-to-market rank, past winners vs. past losers (Chan, Chen, and Lakonishok 2002, Section 5.2 and Table 8)




In Table 8, the losing value funds’ average book-to-market rank falls from 0.648 to 0.572, a move toward growth, while losing growth funds barely move (0.146 to 0.171). The authors read this as managers of poorly performing value funds abandoning a style that has not paid off, while managers of losing growth funds stick with theirs.






TipIs the drift active? A back-of-the-envelope argument



A value fund that lost money holds stocks whose prices fell, so their book-to-market ratios rose. Passive migration alone would push a losing value fund further toward value. Chan, Chen, and Lakonishok find the opposite: losing value funds move toward growth. The direction therefore points to trading, not to stocks migrating under a passive manager. This is our reading of the result, not a test reported in the paper, and it applies to characteristics. With loadings-based ranks, a second force also pulls value funds toward the middle without any trading: mean reversion in estimated ranks (§6.3). A holdings-based decomposition of the change into trades and price movements (Wermers 2012) would test the argument directly.








WarningA referee’s view of the evidence



The paper is exploratory, and its authors say so. Four objections are worth having in mind before you build on it.

Survivorship. The sample is funds alive at the end of 1997. If losing funds that changed style were more likely to survive (or less likely), “losers drift” is partly a statement about which losers survived. A replication on the CRSP survivor-bias-free database removes this concern.
Mean reversion in ranks. Funds sorted into the extreme style groups on estimated ranks are partly there because of estimation noise, so their future ranks drift back toward the middle even if nothing changes. Comparing winners with losers within the same style group nets this out only if noise is unrelated to past performance. §6.3 shows that it is not.
No inference on the key contrasts. The winner-loser comparison and the growth-value alpha gap are descriptive sorts; standard errors for the differences themselves are not reported.
Drift is not a decision. A rank change mixes trading, stock migration, and measurement error. Separating them needs holdings and trades.






6.3 Rebuilding the Design on Simulated Funds
The best way to understand a research design is to run it on data where you know the answer. We simulate a cross-section of funds around several formation dates, estimate three-factor loadings in the 36 months before and the 36 months after each date, and compute the two statistics of Chan et al. (2002): consistency of ranks (their Table 3) and the change in book-to-market rank by past performance (their Table 8).
We run the design twice:

No drift. Every fund’s true loadings move only by a small random amount between the two windows. Any measured “drift” is noise plus that random evolution.
Losers drift. Same, except that value funds in the bottom 20% of past two-year returns cut their HML loading by 0.15 in the second window, the behavior Chan, Chen, and Lakonishok describe.

The factors and fund returns are simulated, so the chunk needs no data.


Code
simulate_ccl <- function(n_funds = 800, n_dates = 100, drift = TRUE, seed = 2002,
                         shift = 0.15, sd_evolve = 0.15) {
  set.seed(seed)
  map(seq_len(n_dates), \(dt) {
    # 72 months of factor returns around one formation date (36 before, 36 after)
    f <- cbind(MKT = rnorm(72, 0.006, 0.045),
               SMB = rnorm(72, 0.002, 0.030),
               HML = rnorm(72, 0.003, 0.030))

    # True style in the past window
    b0 <- rnorm(n_funds, 1.00, 0.12)
    s0 <- rnorm(n_funds, 0.10, 0.35)            # SMB loading: high = small cap
    h0 <- rnorm(n_funds, -0.05, 0.30)           # HML loading: high = value
    sd_e <- runif(n_funds, 0.008, 0.020)        # idiosyncratic volatility

    past <- 1:36; fut <- 37:72
    E <- matrix(rnorm(72 * n_funds), 72, n_funds) %*% diag(sd_e)
    R_past <- f[past, ] %*% rbind(b0, s0, h0) + E[past, ]

    # Past two-year return (months 13-36) decides who is a winner or a loser
    ret24  <- apply(R_past[13:36, ], 2, \(r) prod(1 + r) - 1)
    loser  <- ret24 <= quantile(ret24, 0.2)
    value0 <- h0 >= quantile(h0, 0.7)

    # True style in the future window: everyone evolves a little;
    # under the drift rule, losing value funds also tilt toward growth
    s1 <- s0 + rnorm(n_funds, 0, sd_evolve)
    h1 <- h0 + rnorm(n_funds, 0, sd_evolve) - if (drift) shift * (loser & value0) else 0
    R_fut <- f[fut, ] %*% rbind(b0, s1, h1) + E[fut, ]

    # Three-factor OLS for all funds at once, separately in each window
    ols <- function(R, F) {
      X <- cbind(1, F)
      solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, R))     # 4 x n_funds: alpha, MKT, SMB, HML
    }
    B_past <- ols(R_past, f[past, ]); B_fut <- ols(R_fut, f[fut, ])

    tibble(date = dt, fid = seq_len(n_funds), ret24 = ret24,
           # size rank: 1 = largest (most negative SMB loading); B/M rank: 1 = most value
           size_past = percent_rank(-B_past[3, ]), size_fut = percent_rank(-B_fut[3, ]),
           btm_past  = percent_rank( B_past[4, ]), btm_fut  = percent_rank( B_fut[4, ]))
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

ccl_none  <- simulate_ccl(drift = FALSE)
ccl_drift <- simulate_ccl(drift = TRUE)


The two summary functions follow the paper’s definitions: style groups are the top and bottom 30% of the past rank, winners and losers are the top and bottom 20% of past two-year return, and statistics are computed date by date and then averaged across dates.


Code
# Analogue of CCL Table 3: consistency of style ranks, by style group
consistency_table <- function(d) {
  groups <- list(
    "All funds" = rep(TRUE, nrow(d)),
    "Large cap" = d$size_past >= 0.7, "Small cap" = d$size_past <= 0.3,
    "Value"     = d$btm_past  >= 0.7, "Growth"    = d$btm_past  <= 0.3
  )
  imap(groups, \(g, nm) {
    d[g, ] |>
      summarise(size_corr = cor(size_past, size_fut), size_absdiff = mean(abs(size_fut - size_past)),
                btm_corr  = cor(btm_past,  btm_fut),  btm_absdiff  = mean(abs(btm_fut  - btm_past)),
                .by = date) |>
      summarise(across(-date, mean)) |>
      mutate(group = nm, .before = 1)
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

# Analogue of CCL Table 8: change in B/M rank by past performance and style
loser_table <- function(d) {
  d |>
    mutate(perf  = case_when(ret24 >= quantile(ret24, 0.8) ~ "Winners (top 20%)",
                             ret24 <= quantile(ret24, 0.2) ~ "Losers (bottom 20%)"),
           style = case_when(btm_past >= 0.7 ~ "Value", btm_past <= 0.3 ~ "Growth",
                             TRUE ~ "Middle"),
           .by = date) |>
    filter(!is.na(perf)) |>
    summarise(n = n(), absdiff = mean(abs(btm_fut - btm_past)),   # before btm_* are overwritten
              btm_past = mean(btm_past), btm_fut = mean(btm_fut), .by = c(perf, style)) |>
    mutate(style = factor(style, c("Value", "Middle", "Growth")),
           perf  = factor(perf, c("Winners (top 20%)", "Losers (bottom 20%)"))) |>
    arrange(style, perf)
}

Read the two panels together, starting with the one where nobody drifts.

Extreme groups revert. Value funds’ average rank falls and growth funds’ rises between the two windows, for winners and losers alike. A fund ranked in the top 30% on an estimated loading is there partly by luck, so its next rank is closer to the middle. A move “toward growth” by value funds is therefore expected even with no change in strategy.
Losers and winners do not revert equally. Even with no drift, losing value funds move more than winning value funds, and among growth funds the pattern flips: winners move more. The reason is that past performance depends on the true loading. In the simulation the value premium is positive on average. Among funds with a high estimated HML loading, those whose true loading is lower than estimated earn less of the premium, so they are over-represented among losers; their inflated ranks then fall back. Among growth funds, the funds whose true loading is higher than estimated earn more of the premium and are over-represented among winners. Sorting on past performance therefore sorts partly on measurement error.

With the drift rule switched on, the losing value funds move much further and in the direction of growth, which is the pattern in CCL’s Table 8, and the value-fund gap grows well beyond its no-drift level. The lesson for reading the paper is that the right null is not a gap of zero: a winner-loser gap of the mechanical kind arises without any manager decision, its sign depends on whether the value premium was positive in the ranking period, and it predicts the mirror pattern among growth funds. A careful replication would estimate this null (for instance, with a placebo that re-sorts on returns from a period that does not overlap the loading window) and test the observed gap against it.






NoteWhat the simulation does not settle



The simulation shows that the design can detect drift by losers, and that part of the winner-loser gap it reports is mechanical. It cannot tell you whether real funds drift, whether the funds that drift are the ones that survive, or whether the drift is active or passive. Those questions need real data: the CRSP survivor-bias-free database for the first two, and holdings for the third. Holdings-based characteristics, the paper’s preferred measure, also suffer much less from estimation noise than 36-month loadings, so the mechanical gap should be smaller with them.




6.4 Stated Drift: Label Changes in CRSP
Chan et al. (2002) never use vendor labels; both of their measures are revealed styles. Most CRSP studies, however, start from the labels, because they are available for every fund in every year. How often do the labels move?
We compare each fund’s Lipper objective code with the previous year’s code, for consecutive years only (the filters in Section 3 can leave gaps, and a change across a gap is not an annual change).


Code
transitions <- fund_year |>
  filter(!is.na(lipper_obj_cd)) |>
  arrange(wficn, year) |>
  mutate(prev_cd = lag(lipper_obj_cd), prev_year = lag(year), .by = wficn) |>
  filter(!is.na(prev_cd), year - prev_year == 1) |>
  mutate(switched = lipper_obj_cd != prev_cd)

drift_by_type <- transitions |>
  summarise(
    n_funds        = n_distinct(wficn),
    n_transitions  = n(),
    annual_rate    = mean(switched),
    .by = fund_type
  ) |>
  left_join(
    transitions |>
      summarise(ever = any(switched), .by = c(wficn, fund_type)) |>
      summarise(ever_share = mean(ever), .by = fund_type),
    by = "fund_type"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(annual_rate))

  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(n_funds, n_transitions), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(annual_rate, ever_share), decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(fund_type = "Fund type", n_funds = "Funds",
             n_transitions = "Fund-year transitions",

  tab_header(title = "How Often Does the Stated Style Change?",

NoteReading this in the simulation



In the simulated panel, broad active funds can change style (a 4% chance of a new draw each year), sector funds keep one sector, and true index funds keep one label for life. The table recovers that pattern, with two lessons. First, the Active rate is diluted because the group includes sector funds that never switch. Second, the Index rate is not zero even though no true index fund ever changes style: the switches come from a few active funds whose names contain a trap (a name ending in “RSP”, or “100” in “Select 100 Opportunities”) and so were classified as index funds in Section 4. A classification error leaks directly into a drift statistic. In real CRSP data, label changes among index funds also come from coding noise (a vendor revises a category, or a fund appears under a different code for one year), so a nonzero index-fund switch rate is a data-quality diagnostic, not evidence that the index fund drifted.


Where do funds go when they switch? A transition matrix, row by row, shows the destination style given the origin style.


Code
trans_mat <- transitions |>
  filter(fund_type == "Active") |>
  mutate(from = lump_style(prev_cd), to = lump_style(lipper_obj_cd)) |>
  count(from, to) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n), .by = from) |>
  complete(from, to, fill = list(n = 0L, share = 0)) |>
  mutate(share = round(share, 3))




Code
hchart(trans_mat, "heatmap", hcaes(x = to, y = from, value = share)) |>
  hc_title(text = "Where do active funds go next year?") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = "Style next year")) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Style this year"), reversed = TRUE) |>
  hc_colorAxis(min = 0, max = 1) |>
  hc_plotOptions(series = list(dataLabels = list(enabled = TRUE, format = "{point.value:.2f}"))) |>
  hc_tooltip(pointFormat = "P(<b>{point.y}</b> to <b>{point.x}</b>) = {point.value:.3f}")








Figure 12: Transition probabilities between stated styles (active funds): origin on the vertical axis, destination on the horizontal axis




The diagonal dominates: most funds keep their label from one year to the next, as they should. The off-diagonal cells show which styles funds migrate between. With real data, look at whether the largest off-diagonal cells connect adjacent categories (growth to growth-and-income, mid-cap to small-cap). If they do, many of the switches may be a vendor re-labeling a fund whose portfolio has barely changed. That is why stated drift is a good first screen but a poor final measure.


6.5 Revealed Drift in Individual Funds
Chan et al. (2002) compare a fund’s style in two non-overlapping windows, which is what a cross-sectional study needs. To watch one fund’s style move, we instead estimate its exposures month by month in a rolling window. Two tools are common, and we run both on public data so that you can reproduce them without CRSP.

Rolling Carhart loadings (Lecture 1): regress monthly excess returns on the four factors in a rolling 36-month window. Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) use the lagged version of these rolling betas to split fund returns into a style component and a residual.
Sharpe style weights (Sharpe 1992): regress the fund’s returns on a handful of style index returns, constrained so the weights are non-negative and sum to one, so the weights read as “this fund behaves like 70% large growth and 30% small growth”.


Data


Code
start_date <- "2005-01-01"
end_date   <- "2025-12-31"

# Four style "corners" (Russell 1000/2000 growth and value ETFs) as the style indexes
style_etfs   <- c(LG = "IWF", LV = "IWD", SG = "IWO", SV = "IWN")
style_labels <- c(LG = "Large growth", LV = "Large value", SG = "Small growth", SV = "Small value")

# Four long-lived mutual funds to analyze (you can change these tickers)
drift_funds  <- c(FMAGX = "Fidelity Magellan", FCNTX = "Fidelity Contrafund",
                  AGTHX = "Growth Fund of America", VWNDX = "Vanguard Windsor")

# unname(): a named vector would make tq_get() use the first name ("LG") as the
# column name instead of "symbol"
px_raw <- tq_get(unname(c(style_etfs, names(drift_funds))),
                 from = start_date, to = end_date, get = "stock.prices")

px_ret <- px_raw |>
  group_by(symbol) |>
  tq_transmute(select = adjusted, mutate_fun = periodReturn,
               period = "monthly", type = "arithmetic", col_rename = "ret") |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(ym = lubridate::floor_date(date, "month")) |>
  select(symbol, ym, ret)

# Kenneth French's factors (monthly, in percent)
ff3_raw <- download_french_data("Fama/French 3 Factors")
mom_raw <- download_french_data("Momentum Factor (Mom)")

ff4 <- ff3_raw$subsets$data[[1]] |>
  mutate(ym = lubridate::floor_date(lubridate::ym(date), "month"),
         across(c(`Mkt-RF`, SMB, HML, RF), \(x) x / 100)) |>
  rename(RMRF = `Mkt-RF`) |>
  select(ym, RMRF, SMB, HML, RF) |>
  inner_join(
    mom_raw$subsets$data[[1]] |>
      mutate(ym = lubridate::floor_date(lubridate::ym(date), "month"), UMD = Mom / 100) |>
      select(ym, UMD),
    by = "ym"
  )




Code
# One row per month: style ETFs, funds, and factors
ret_wide <- px_ret |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = symbol, values_from = ret) |>
  inner_join(ff4, by = "ym") |>
  filter(ym >= as.Date(start_date), ym <= as.Date(end_date)) |>
  drop_na(all_of(c(unname(style_etfs), "RMRF", "SMB", "HML", "UMD", "RF"))) |>
  arrange(ym)

# Style-return matrix with columns named by style code (LG, LV, SG, SV), not by ticker.
# Renaming inside select() keeps the names tied to the tickers they belong to.
X_style <- ret_wide |>
  select(LG = all_of(style_etfs[["LG"]]), LV = all_of(style_etfs[["LV"]]),
         SG = all_of(style_etfs[["SG"]]), SV = all_of(style_etfs[["SV"]])) |>
  as.matrix()
stopifnot(nrow(X_style) == nrow(ret_wide),
          identical(colnames(X_style), c("LG", "LV", "SG", "SV")))

cat("Months:", nrow(ret_wide), "from", format(min(ret_wide$ym)), "to", format(max(ret_wide$ym)), "\n")


Months: 252 from 2005-01-01 to 2025-12-01 




The Estimators


Code
# Sharpe (1992): min ||y - Xw||^2  s.t.  w >= 0, sum(w) = 1  (no intercept)
sharpe_weights <- function(y, X) {
  y <- 100 * y; X <- 100 * X                       # percent units keep the QP well scaled
  k    <- ncol(X)
  sol  <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * crossprod(X) + diag(1e-8, k),
                             dvec = 2 * crossprod(X, y),
                             Amat = cbind(rep(1, k), diag(k)),
                             bvec = c(1, rep(0, k)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  w / sum(w)
}

# Rolling Sharpe weights; the weight for month t uses months t-width+1 ... t
roll_style <- function(y, X, dates, width = 36) {
  map(width:length(y), \(i) {
    idx <- (i - width + 1):i
    tibble(ym = dates[i], style = colnames(X),
           w  = sharpe_weights(y[idx], X[idx, , drop = FALSE]))
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

# Rolling Carhart loadings
roll_carhart <- function(d, width = 36) {          # d: ym, ex (excess return), RMRF, SMB, HML, UMD
  map(width:nrow(d), \(i) {
    b <- coef(lm(ex ~ RMRF + SMB + HML + UMD, data = d[(i - width + 1):i, ]))
    tibble(ym = d$ym[i], Mkt = b[["RMRF"]], SMB = b[["SMB"]], HML = b[["HML"]], UMD = b[["UMD"]])
  }) |> list_rbind()
}




Validate first: a fund whose style we control
Before applying an estimator to real funds, apply it to a fund whose true style we know. We build a synthetic fund from the real style-ETF returns. Until the end of 2015 it holds 70% large growth and 30% small growth; from January 2016 it switches to 70% large value and 30% small value. A little noise stands in for stock selection. A good estimator should recover the switch.


Code
switch_date <- as.Date("2016-01-01")

set.seed(3)
post <- ret_wide$ym >= switch_date

# True weights as a matrix with the same rows and columns as X_style
W_true_mat <- cbind(LG = if_else(post, 0, 0.7), LV = if_else(post, 0.7, 0),
                    SG = if_else(post, 0, 0.3), SV = if_else(post, 0.3, 0))
W_true_mat <- W_true_mat[, colnames(X_style), drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(identical(dim(W_true_mat), dim(X_style)))

synth_ret <- rowSums(W_true_mat * X_style) +
  rnorm(nrow(X_style), 0, 0.0025)       # 25 bp monthly noise = "stock selection"

W_true <- bind_cols(tibble(ym = ret_wide$ym), as_tibble(W_true_mat))

W_est <- roll_style(synth_ret, X_style, ret_wide$ym, width = 36)

# Share of weight placed on the right side of the switch, month by month
est_check <- W_est |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = style, values_from = w) |>
  mutate(est_growth = LG + SG, true_growth = if_else(ym < switch_date, 1, 0))

W_true_long <- W_true |>
  pivot_longer(-ym, names_to = "style", values_to = "w") |>
  mutate(style = unname(style_labels[style]))
W_est_long <- W_est |>
  mutate(style = unname(style_labels[style]), w = round(w, 3))

switch_ts <- as.numeric(as.POSIXct(switch_date, tz = "UTC")) * 1000   # highcharts uses ms




Code
hchart(W_true_long, "area", hcaes(x = ym, y = w, group = style)) |>
  hc_title(text = "True weights: growth until 2015, value from 2016") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL)) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Weight"), max = 1) |>
  hc_plotOptions(area = list(stacking = "normal", marker = list(enabled = FALSE))) |>
  hc_tooltip(shared = TRUE, pointFormat = "{series.name}: <b>{point.y:.2f}</b><br/>")

Code
hchart(W_est_long, "area", hcaes(x = ym, y = w, group = style)) |>
  hc_title(text = "Estimated weights: rolling 36-month window") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL),
           plotLines = list(list(value = switch_ts, color = "#E15759", width = 2, dashStyle = "Dash",
                                 label = list(text = "True switch", rotation = 0)))) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Weight"), max = 1) |>
  hc_plotOptions(area = list(stacking = "normal", marker = list(enabled = FALSE))) |>
  hc_tooltip(shared = TRUE, pointFormat = "{series.name}: <b>{point.y:.2f}</b><br/>")








Figure 14: Rolling 36-month Sharpe style weights recovered from the synthetic fund’s returns




The estimator finds the switch, but it finds it late and gradually. A window of 36 months mixes old and new months until the old months have rolled out, so the estimated weights move for about three years after the true change. This is the central trade-off of every rolling-window drift measure: a short window reacts fast but is noisy, a long window is stable but slow. A related design choice: Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) use lagged betas (estimated through the previous month) when they build the style component of a return, so that the style measure does not use the return being explained.


Code
# How many months after the true switch does the estimated growth weight fall below 50%?
first_below <- est_check |> filter(ym >= switch_date, est_growth < 0.5) |> slice_head(n = 1) |> pull(ym)
cat("Estimated growth weight falls below 50% in", format(first_below, "%b %Y"),
    "-", round(time_length(first_below - switch_date, "month")), "months after the true switch.\n")


Estimated growth weight falls below 50% in Mar 2017 - 14 months after the true switch.




Real funds: rolling style weights


Code

  d <- ret_wide |> select(ym, y = all_of(s)) |> drop_na()
  X <- X_style[match(d$ym, ret_wide$ym), , drop = FALSE]
  roll_style(d$y, X, d$ym, width = 36) |> mutate(symbol = s)
}) |> list_rbind() |>
  mutate(fund = unname(drift_funds[symbol]), style = unname(style_labels[style]), w = round(w, 3))

To look at another fund, change the ticker in the filter(symbol == ...) call. Two cautions apply to every chart of this kind. The four ETFs are correlated, so a few percentage points of weight can move between neighbors without changing the fit; do not over-read small wiggles. And the weights describe behavior, not holdings: a fund that holds cash or non-US stocks will have that part of its return mapped onto whichever style index it happens to resemble.


Real funds: rolling Carhart loadings


Code
carhart_roll <- map(names(drift_funds), \(s) {
  d <- ret_wide |> select(ym, ret = all_of(s), RMRF, SMB, HML, UMD, RF) |>
    drop_na() |> mutate(ex = ret - RF)

}) |> list_rbind() |>
  mutate(fund = unname(drift_funds[symbol]),

6.6 A Number for Drift: Style Turnover
Charts are good for a handful of funds. A study of thousands of funds needs one number per fund and year. A simple choice is style turnover: the distance between a fund’s style weights today and twelve months ago,
\[
\text{StyleTurnover}_{i,t} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\left| w_{i,s,t} - w_{i,s,t-12} \right|.
\tag{1}
\]
It equals the fraction of the portfolio that would have to be reassigned to a different style to get from last year’s weights to this year’s. It is 0 for a fund that never changes style and 1 for a fund that moved entirely from one style to another. Because the weights come from a rolling window, the measure is smooth and has the lag we saw above. It is a measure we construct for teaching. It is the within-fund cousin of the mean absolute change in style rank in Chan et al. (2002): theirs measures how far a fund moves relative to other funds, ours how far its own style weights move. Both inherit the noise floor of §6.3.


Code
style_turnover <- fund_style |>
  arrange(symbol, style, ym) |>
  mutate(w_lag = lag(w, 12), .by = c(symbol, style)) |>
  filter(!is.na(w_lag)) |>
  summarise(turnover = 0.5 * sum(abs(w - w_lag)), .by = c(fund, symbol, ym)) |>
  mutate(turnover = round(turnover, 3))

turnover_summary <- style_turnover |>
  summarise(mean_turnover = mean(turnover), max_turnover = max(turnover),
            share_above_30 = mean(turnover > 0.3), .by = fund) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_turnover))

WarningFive traps in drift measurement




Noise looks like drift. Estimation error in rolling or windowed loadings produces movement even for a fund whose style never changes. Always run the estimator on synthetic funds with a known, constant style to calibrate the noise floor before interpreting any number (§6.3, §6.5).
Extreme groups revert. Funds sorted into the top or bottom of an estimated style ranking move back toward the middle next period without any decision. A “move toward growth” by value funds is partly this.
Sorting on performance sorts on noise. Past returns depend on true style, so winners and losers differ in how much of their estimated style is error. A winner-loser gap in drift has a mechanical component whose sign depends on the realized style premium (§6.3).
Label changes are not portfolio changes. A vendor can re-code a fund because its own taxonomy changed. Check the filled and unfilled codes (Section 3.3, step 2) before counting a switch.
Drift is conditional on the benchmark set. Style weights depend on which style indexes are in the regression. With four corners, a fund that holds mid-cap stocks is a blend of large and small. Report the style set with the result.

title: Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
section: 7. Putting It Together: A Replication Checklist
text:
7. Putting It Together: A Replication Checklist
Use this list every time you start a new mutual fund study. Each item names the problem it prevents.

Start from the right unit. Work at the fund (WFICN) level unless the question is about share classes. Sum TNA across classes; take the age of the oldest class; TNA-weight the expense ratio and fees.
Remove incubation. Drop the first years of life (three, following Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026); 18 months in Doshi et al. (2015)). Use the oldest class’s first offer date.
Remove tiny funds. TNA below $15 million (Elton et al. 2001), as a size filter in addition to the age filter.
Validate missing and sentinel values. CRSP stores missing expense ratios as -99 and has implausible values; handle them before aggregating.
Restrict to domestic equity and say how. Vendor codes, name screens (foreign names), and a minimum share of years in domestic equity.
Remove what is not an active equity fund. ETNs, leveraged and inverse funds, target-date funds (Parker et al. 2023), and either index funds or active ETFs, depending on the question.
Parse names with word boundaries, not substrings. Test every regex on a list of known true and false positives.
Fill style codes deliberately. Document how you carry codes forward and backward, and check the result against the unfilled series.
Report the attrition table. Funds and observations after each step. Readers can then see which filter drives the result.
Report robustness. Re-run the main result with a different classification recipe and a different age cutoff.
Measure drift against a null, not against zero. Calibrate the noise floor of any drift measure on synthetic funds with a known style, and test winner-loser differences against a placebo sort.

title: Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
text:
8. Key Takeaways

The sample is the first model. Filters are not housekeeping: each one removes a documented bias, and the incubation simulation shows that skipping one can turn zero skill into apparent skill.
Share classes are not funds. Aggregate to the fund level before counting funds, assigning age, or averaging fees.
Three recipes, three universes. Doshi et al. (2015), Back et al. (2018), and Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) agree on core active equity funds and disagree at the edges (index funds, hedged strategies, sector funds, name parsing). Use the recipe that fits the question, and report how much your result moves with another.
Names are data, but dirty data. A regex that works on ten fund names fails on ten thousand; test with true and false positives.
Stated and revealed style are different objects. The stated label is cheap and universal; revealed style is harder but reflects what the fund does.
Styles cluster near the market and persist imperfectly (Chan et al. 2002). Funds that change style are disproportionately past losers, especially value funds moving toward growth.
A drift statistic needs the right null. Estimated ranks revert, and sorting on past performance sorts partly on estimation error, so part of a winner-loser gap is mechanical. Rolling-window measures also trade speed for noise. Validate every estimator on funds whose true style you set.
Not all style change is a decision. Stocks migrate across style boundaries, and vendors re-label funds; only holdings and trades can separate active from passive drift.

title: Lecture 3: Fund Classification, Style, and Style Drift
text:
9. Discussion Questions

The incubation simulation sets true alpha to zero for every fund. Explain, in terms of the selection rule that decides which funds are released, why the released funds still show a positive average alpha during incubation. Why does the alpha vanish once the funds are public, and what does this imply for studies that include the incubation years?
Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026) drop the first three years of a fund’s life, while Doshi et al. (2015) drop 18 months. Design a test to choose between the two windows. What would you compare, and what does a “too short” window look like in your test?
The TNA filter of $15 million is applied to the fund after the share classes are summed. What would change if it were applied to each share class instead? Which funds would be dropped that should be kept, and which kept that should be dropped?
Compare the active-fund counts of the three recipes in the simulation (Table 3). For the funds that only one recipe flags, which true type are they? What do the differences imply for a paper whose result is about “active funds”?
A name filter contains the pattern ind to catch “Index” and “Ind” funds. Give three fund names for which the filter makes the wrong call. How would you test the filter before using it on the full sample?
In the simulation, the stated-drift table shows a nonzero label-switch rate for the Index group even though no true index fund changes style. We traced it to one cause (name-parsing errors). List three other reasons a real index fund could show a label change that are not “the fund changed its style”. How would you tell them apart?
In the rolling-window validation (§6.5), the rolling estimate takes roughly half the window length to register a style change that happened in a single month. A shorter window would react sooner. What do you lose with the shorter window? Propose a way to choose the window length from the data.
Equation (1) and the mean absolute rank change in Chan et al. (2002) are both computed from styles estimated with error. If the true style never changes, is the expected value of either measure zero? Use the “No drift” panel of Table 9 to explain, and propose a way to remove the bias.
A fund that keeps its “growth” label while its returns load on HML like a value fund is a case of revealed drift without stated drift. What are two reasons the manager might leave the label unchanged, and how would each affect your inference in a study of flows?
In Table 10, losing value funds move more than winning value funds even when no fund changes style, and the pattern flips for growth funds. Explain the mechanism. Would the sign of this mechanical gap change in a period when the value premium was negative? Modify simulate_ccl() to check, and say what this implies for comparing Chan et al. (2002)’s 1984–1994 sample with a post-2007 sample.
Chan et al. (2002) study funds alive at the end of 1997. Describe how you would redo their Table 8 on the CRSP survivor-bias-free database. Which result would most change your reading of “losers drift”: losers that drift being more likely to survive, or less likely? Why?

title: Slides 03: Fund Classification and Style Drift
text:
Incubation: how zero skill becomes “skill”
A family seeds several funds privately, then opens only the winners to the public; the private record is backfilled (Evans 2010).






Incubated funds’ alpha: 1.7% per year with the backfilled record, 0.2% after dropping the first 36 months.

Simulated, not calibrated. Evans (2010) finds incubated funds outperform non-incubated ones by about 3.5% risk-adjusted while private, and the gap disappears after opening. Link to Lecture 2: this is a selection problem that manufactures false discoveries.

The window is a design choice

Doshi et al. (2015): drop the first 18 months
Back et al. (2018): use returns only after the first offer date and once the fund name appears
Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026): drop the first 3 years — also removes the burst of sentiment-driven ETF launches (Ben-David et al. 2023)


Longer window → safer filter, fewer young funds. Report it, and show robustness to it.

Three ways to know a fund’s style








Approach
Source
Weakness




Stated
Prospectus objective; Lipper / Morningstar / CRSP codes
It is what the fund chooses to say (Kim et al. 2000; Cooper et al. 2005)


Returns-based
Factor loadings; Sharpe (1992) style weights
Needs a long window; lags


Holdings-based
Size, B/M, momentum of stocks held (Daniel et al. 1997)

Style drift = the style moves over time. Two sources: the manager trades into a new style (active), or the stocks migrate while held (passive) (Wermers 2012).

title: Slides 03: Fund Classification and Style Drift
text:
Why researchers care about drift

Benchmarks. A “growth” fund holding value stocks earns an alpha that is a style bet (Lecture 1)
Investors’ portfolios. A growth + value mix only diversifies if each fund stays what it is
Agency. A manager behind in the race may change strategy to catch up (Brown et al. 1996; Chevalier and Ellison 1997) — drift is one way to do it
Sample selection. A paper on “growth funds” studies whatever the label contains

The source paper
Chan et al. (2002) — “On Mutual Fund Investment Styles”, RFS 15(5)


Data

3,336 U.S. domestic equity funds alive at end-1997
Defunct funds only from 1989 → early years are survivor-biased


Two style measures

text:
Finding 2 · Styles persist, but not tightly
Correlation between a fund’s style rank (FF3 loadings) over the past 3 years and over the non-overlapping 3 years after, year-ends 1984–1994 (CCL Table 3):






Correlations of 0.7–0.9, yet the average absolute change in rank is 0.11–0.18 — a fund moves more than a decile, on average, every three years.

title: Slides 03: Fund Classification and Style Drift
text:
Finding 3 · Losers change style
Sort funds on past two-year return (winners = top 20%, losers = bottom 20%) and on style (top / middle / bottom 30%); measure the absolute change in B/M rank (CCL Section 5.2, Table 8).






Losing value funds drift twice as far as winning ones — and toward growth (B/M rank 0.648 → 0.572). Losing growth funds stay put (0.146 → 0.171).

The paper’s reading: style shifts are concentrated among poor performers and driven by value funds. Note this is a descriptive sort; the paper does not report standard errors on these differences.

title: Slides 03: Fund Classification and Style Drift
section: Is that drift active? A quick argument
text:
Is that drift active? A quick argument
A value fund that lost money holds stocks whose prices fell → their B/M ratios rose.

Passive migration alone would push a losing value fund further toward value.


CCL find losing value funds move toward growth — against the passive channel. For holdings characteristics, that points to trading, consistent with a manager abandoning a style that has not paid off.


(This is our reading of the result, not a test in the paper. Holdings changes are what separate active from passive drift (Wermers 2012).)

text:
Finding 4 · Style-adjusted performance
Equal-weighted alphas of size × B/M fund groups (CCL Table 6 and conclusion):

Growth minus value: about 0.143% per month (≈ 1.7% per year) under three factors
About 1.2% per year after adding momentum
Concentrated in small-cap funds: 2.82% per year four-factor gap


The authors call this “some evidence.” The difference itself carries no reported standard error, and the sample conditions on survival to 1997.

text:
Why loadings lag: a fund we control
A simulated fund holds 70% large growth + 30% small growth, then switches entirely to value at month 121. Rolling 36-month Sharpe weights:






The estimate crosses 50% only 17 months after the switch. Short windows react faster but are noisier — the core trade-off in every returns-based drift measure.

title: Slides 03: Fund Classification and Style Drift
text:
A referee’s view of CCL (2002)

Survivorship. The sample is funds alive at end-1997. Losers that survived may be precisely those that changed style — drift and survival are jointly selected
Mean reversion and a mechanical gap. Estimated extreme ranks revert, and past returns depend on true style, so losers and winners differ in how noisy their ranks are. In a simulation with no drift, value losers still move ~0.016 more than value winners (handout §6.3) — the null is not zero
No inference on the key contrasts. Table 8 and the growth–value alpha gap are descriptive sorts
Drift ≠ decision. Rank changes mix trading, stock migration, and estimation error; separating them needs holdings and trades


Ask the class which objection is most damaging and what data would address it. Natural follow-ups: CRSP survivor-bias-free data, holdings-based decomposition (Wermers 2012), a placebo using a synthetic constant-style fund to calibrate the noise floor.

title: Slides 03: Fund Classification and Style Drift
text:
Key takeaways

The sample is the first model. Each filter removes a documented bias; skipping incubation turns zero skill into apparent skill
Share classes are not funds. Aggregate to WFICN before counting, aging, or averaging fees
Three recipes, three populations. They agree on the core and disagree at the edges; report robustness to a second recipe
Styles cluster near the market and persist imperfectly (Chan et al. 2002)
Losers drift, especially value losers moving toward growth
Holdings beat loadings for measuring current style; loadings lag by construction

title: Slides 03: Fund Classification and Style Drift
text:
Discussion questions

Survivorship: how would you redo CCL’s Table 8 with the CRSP survivor-bias-free database? What result would change your conclusion?
Design a test that separates active drift (trading) from passive drift (stock migration) for a value fund that lost money.
A fund keeps its “growth” label while its returns load like a value fund. Why might the manager leave the label unchanged? How would that bias a study of fund flows?

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
text:
Lectures 1 and 2 asked how well managers perform and whether the performance is skill. Lecture 3 asked which funds belong in the sample and what kind of funds they are. This lecture turns from the manager to the investor: how does money move between funds, and how does it respond to performance?
The question matters because of how a fund company is paid. Its revenue is
\[
\text{Revenue}_{i,t} = f_i \times \text{TNA}_{i,t},
\tag{1}
\]
where \(f_i\) is the expense ratio and TNA is total net assets. Fees change rarely, so revenue grows mainly through TNA, and TNA grows in two ways: the return on the assets already in the fund, and flows, the new money investors put in or take out. The way flows respond to performance is therefore the fund company’s implicit incentive contract. It is written by investors, not by the board, and it shapes what managers do. Berk and Green (2004), which we met in Lecture 2, is a model in which this response is what competes skill away.
We work with 100 randomly selected active U.S. domestic equity funds from the CRSP Survivor-Bias-Free Mutual Fund Database, observed monthly from 2000 to 2025 at the fund (class-group) level. The lecture has three parts.

Measure flows. We compute fund-level flows, see which problems survive the aggregation of share classes into funds, and decide what to filter.
Estimate the flow–performance relationship. We review the theory and the evidence (Sirri and Tufano (1998) and what followed), then run a replication-style version of the Sirri and Tufano (1998) regression on the 100 funds, ask which performance measure explains flows best, and look at young funds and at funds that disappear.
Ask whether the shape is behavior or design. The headline result of the literature is that flows are convex in performance. Spiegel and Zhang (2013) argue that this convexity is an artifact of how the regression is run. We simulate an industry three times to see when the standard estimator recovers the true shape and when it manufactures one.







NoteWhat moved out of this lecture



The tournament and risk-shifting tests (Brown et al. (1996), Busse (2001), Schwarz (2012)), which an earlier draft paired with flows, move to the next lecture. They take the shape of the flow function as given, so they need what we build here first.


By the end of the lecture, you should be able to:

compute dollar and percentage flows from fund-level TNA and returns, and explain each requirement (consecutive months, a valid return, a minimum lagged TNA);
recognize what a flow is not: mergers, share-class launches, reporting gaps, cash distributions, and liquidations;
summarize the evidence on the shape of the flow–performance relationship and on which performance measure investors respond to;
estimate the Sirri and Tufano (1998) piecewise-linear regression and test for convexity;
explain, with data and with simulations, why survivorship and heterogeneous investors can produce convexity when no investor behaves convexly.
