Fees change rarely, so revenue grows mainly through TNA, and TNA grows in two ways: the return on the assets already in the fund, and flows, the new money investors put in or take out. The way flows respond to performance is therefore the fund company’s implicit incentive contract. It is written by investors, not by the board, and it shapes what managers do. Berk and Green (2004), which we met in Lecture 2, is a model in which this response is what competes skill away.
We work with 100 randomly selected active U.S. domestic equity funds from the CRSP Survivor-Bias-Free Mutual Fund Database, observed monthly from 2000 to 2025 at the fund (class-group) level. The lecture has three parts.

Measure flows. We compute fund-level flows, see which problems survive the aggregation of share classes into funds, and decide what to filter.
Estimate the flow–performance relationship. We review the theory and the evidence (Sirri and Tufano (1998) and what followed), then run a replication-style version of the Sirri and Tufano (1998) regression on the 100 funds, ask which performance measure explains flows best, and look at young funds and at funds that disappear.
Ask whether the shape is behavior or design. The headline result of the literature is that flows are convex in performance. Spiegel and Zhang (2013) argue that this convexity is an artifact of how the regression is run. We simulate an industry three times to see when the standard estimator recovers the true shape and when it manufactures one.







NoteWhat moved out of this lecture



The tournament and risk-shifting tests (Brown et al. (1996), Busse (2001), Schwarz (2012)), which an earlier draft paired with flows, move to the next lecture. They take the shape of the flow function as given, so they need what we build here first.


By the end of the lecture, you should be able to:

compute dollar and percentage flows from fund-level TNA and returns, and explain each requirement (consecutive months, a valid return, a minimum lagged TNA);
recognize what a flow is not: mergers, share-class launches, reporting gaps, cash distributions, and liquidations;
summarize the evidence on the shape of the flow–performance relationship and on which performance measure investors respond to;
estimate the Sirri and Tufano (1998) piecewise-linear regression and test for convexity;
explain, with data and with simulations, why survivorship and heterogeneous investors can produce convexity when no investor behaves convexly.

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
text:
1. Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(highcharter)   # interactive charts
library(gt)
library(DT)
library(fixest)        # panel regressions
library(arrow)         # read the parquet sample
library(frenchdata)    # Kenneth French's Data Library

# Data source for Sections 2 and 4:
#   "crsp"      -> sample_funds_100_clgrp.parquet (built from the licensed CRSP Mutual Fund Database)
#   "simulated" -> a simulated panel with the same columns, for readers without CRSP access
data_source <- "crsp"
pq_path     <- "sample_funds_100_clgrp.parquet"



1.1 The sample
The sample is built by make_fund_sample.R. The script works from two CRSP tables, fund_summary2 (quarterly fund characteristics) and monthly_tna_ret_nav (monthly returns and TNA), and identifies a fund with its CRSP class group, crsp_cl_grp: all share classes of the same portfolio share one class group. It then draws 100 funds at random from those that pass the screens below.

How the 100 funds were selected (make_fund_sample.R)






Screen
Rule




Style
At least 75% of the fund’s CRSP objective codes are diversified domestic equity (EDCL, EDCM, EDCS, EDCI, EDYG, EDYB, EDYI); sector, hedged, and short funds are out


Equity share
Average share of assets in common stock (per_com) of at least 80%


Not passive or packaged
No share class ever carries an index-fund flag, an ETF/ETN flag, a variable-annuity flag, or an index/ETF or target-date/allocation name


History
At least 120 months between 2000 and 2025 with a valid return for at least one share class



Share classes are then aggregated to the class group by month (Part B of the script). TNA is summed across share classes; the fund return ret_vw weights each class’s return by its lagged TNA; expense ratio, management fee, 12b-1 fee, and turnover are lagged-TNA-weighted averages; fund age is measured from the first offer date of the oldest share class. These are the rules of Lecture 3, §2.

Columns of sample_funds_100_clgrp.parquet






Column
Meaning




crsp_cl_grp
CRSP class group (the fund)


caldt
Month-end date


fund_name
Name of the largest share class, class suffix removed


n_class
Number of share classes with a record that month


tna
Fund TNA, sum over share classes ($ millions)


ret_vw
Fund return, share-class returns weighted by lagged class TNA


ret_ew
Fund return, equal-weighted across share classes


exp_ratio, mgmt_fee, actual_12b1, turn_ratio
Lagged-TNA-weighted fees and turnover (decimal)


first_offer
First offer date of the oldest share class


crsp_obj_cd
CRSP objective code of the largest share class


age_years
Fund age in years









WarningWhat the selection rule does to a flow study



The 120-month history requirement keeps only funds that lived at least ten years inside 2000–2025. A fund launched in 2018, or one that was closed after five bad years, cannot be in the sample. Those are exactly the funds with the most extreme flows: young funds, whose flows respond most to performance in the Berk and Green (2004) logic, and dying funds, whose last outflows shape the bottom of the flow function (§4.5 and §5). The database is survivor-bias free; this sample is selected on survival. Keep this in mind whenever a number below looks small.








WarningLicensed data



CRSP data are licensed. The 100-fund file is for use in class. A public version of this handout should be rendered with data_source <- "simulated": the simulator below produces a panel with the same columns and the same kinds of data problems, so every chunk runs unchanged, but its numbers are not CRSP’s.


Performance in Section 4 is measured against factor models, so we need the Fama-French factors. They are public.


Code
ff3_raw <- download_french_data("Fama/French 3 Factors")

ff <- ff3_raw$subsets$data[[1]] |>
  transmute(ym    = floor_date(ym(date), "month"),
            mktrf = `Mkt-RF` / 100,
            smb   = SMB / 100,
            hml   = HML / 100,
            rf    = RF / 100)


The simulator is only used when data_source == "simulated" or when the parquet file is missing. It builds 100 funds whose flows respond convexly to their within-month performance rank, more strongly when the fund is young, and plants the problems we look for in Section 2: share-class launches, one-month reporting gaps, mergers, and funds that wind down before they exit. Skim it.


Code
simulate_clgrp <- function(ff, n_funds = 100, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  mkt <- ff |> filter(ym >= as.Date("2000-01-01"), ym <= as.Date("2025-12-01"))
  n_t <- nrow(mkt)

  obj  <- c("EDCL", "EDCM", "EDCS", "EDCI", "EDYG", "EDYB", "EDYI")
  fam  <- c("Alder", "Beacon", "Cedar", "Delta", "Everest", "Falcon", "Granite", "Harbor",
            "Juniper", "Kestrel")
  word <- c("Growth", "Value", "Opportunities", "Equity Income", "Small Cap", "Mid Cap",
            "Select", "Capital Appreciation", "Core Equity", "Discovery")

  launched <- runif(n_funds) < 0.35                                   # launched after 2000
  start    <- if_else(launched, sample(2:180, n_funds, TRUE), 1L)
  exits    <- runif(n_funds) < 0.30
  end      <- if_else(exits & start + 120 < n_t,
                      map2_int(start, n_t, \(s, n) if (s + 120 < n) sample((s + 120):(n - 1), 1) else n),
                      n_t)
  first_offer <- if_else(launched, mkt$ym[start] - sample(0:25, n_funds, TRUE),
                         as.Date("2000-01-01") - sample(365:(365 * 35), n_funds, TRUE))

  beta <- runif(n_funds, 0.8, 1.2); sd_e <- runif(n_funds, 0.012, 0.03)
  tna0 <- if_else(launched, exp(rnorm(n_funds, log(8), 0.8)), exp(rnorm(n_funds, log(200), 1.5)))
  merger_t <- rep(NA_integer_, n_funds)
  mg <- sample(which(end - start > 60), 3)
  merger_t[mg] <- map_int(mg, \(i) sample((start[i] + 24):(end[i] - 12), 1))

  R   <- matrix(NA_real_, n_funds, n_t); TNA <- R; FL <- R
  ncl <- matrix(NA_integer_, n_funds, n_t)
  for (t in seq_len(n_t)) {
    alive <- start <= t & t <= end
    R[alive, t] <- mkt$rf[t] + beta[alive] * mkt$mktrf[t] + rnorm(sum(alive), 0, sd_e[alive]) -
                   if_else(end[alive] < n_t & end[alive] - t < 36, 0.004, 0)   # funds about to exit underperform
    born <- alive & start == t
    TNA[born, t] <- tna0[born]; ncl[born, t] <- sample(1:4, sum(born), TRUE)
    old <- alive & start < t
    if (!any(old)) next
    has12 <- old & start <= t - 12
    r12 <- rep(NA_real_, n_funds)
    if (t > 12) r12[has12] <- apply(1 + R[has12, (t - 12):(t - 1), drop = FALSE], 1, prod) - 1
    rk  <- rep(NA_real_, n_funds); rk[has12] <- percent_rank(r12[has12])
    seg <- 0.010 * pmin(rk, 0.2) + 0.012 * pmin(0.6, pmax(rk - 0.2, 0)) + 0.060 * pmax(rk - 0.8, 0)
    age <- as.numeric(mkt$ym[t] - first_offer) / 365.25
    f   <- if_else(has12, -0.010 + if_else(age < 6, 1.8, 1) * seg, 0.015) +
           0.25 * coalesce(FL[, t - 1], 0) +
           rnorm(n_funds, 0, 0.008 + 0.04 / sqrt(pmax(coalesce(TNA[, t - 1], 1), 1)))
    f <- f - if_else(end - t < 24 & end < n_t, 0.03, 0)               # funds winding down
    launch_class <- old & runif(n_funds) < 0.004                     # a new share class brings money
    f <- f + if_else(launch_class, runif(n_funds, 0.05, 0.30), 0)
    f <- f + if_else(!is.na(merger_t) & merger_t == t, runif(n_funds, 1, 2.5), 0)
    FL[old, t]  <- f[old]
    ncl[old, t] <- ncl[old, t - 1] + launch_class[old]
    TNA[old, t] <- pmax(0.1, TNA[old, t - 1] * (1 + R[old, t]) * (1 + f[old]))
  }

  out <- map(seq_len(n_funds), \(i) {
    idx <- start[i]:end[i]
    tibble(crsp_cl_grp = 3000000 + i, ym = mkt$ym[idx], n_class = ncl[i, idx],
           tna = TNA[i, idx], ret = R[i, idx])
  }) |> list_rbind()

  chars <- tibble(crsp_cl_grp = 3000000 + seq_len(n_funds),
                  fund_name   = paste(sample(fam, n_funds, TRUE), sample(word, n_funds, TRUE), "Fund"),
                  first_offer = first_offer,
                  crsp_obj_cd = sample(obj, n_funds, TRUE, c(.2, .12, .12, .03, .25, .2, .08)),
                  er0 = pmax(0.002, rnorm(n_funds, 0.0115, 0.003)),
                  b12 = sample(c(0, 0.0025, 0.005, 0.0075), n_funds, TRUE),
                  turn0 = exp(rnorm(n_funds, log(0.6), 0.6)))

  out |>
    left_join(chars, by = "crsp_cl_grp") |>
    mutate(# one-month reporting gap: a share class's TNA is missing, so the fund total dips
           gap   = runif(n()) < 0.003 & ym > min(ym) & ym < max(ym),
           tna   = round(if_else(gap, tna * (1 - runif(n(), 0.2, 0.6)), tna), 1),
           .by = crsp_cl_grp) |>
    mutate(ret_vw = if_else(ym == min(ym), NA_real_, ret),           # no lagged class TNA in month 1
           ret_ew = ret + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.0003),
           exp_ratio   = round(er0 - 0.00002 * (as.numeric(ym - min(ym)) / 30), 4),
           mgmt_fee    = round(0.65 * exp_ratio, 4),
           actual_12b1 = b12,
           turn_ratio  = round(turn0 * exp(rnorm(n(), 0, 0.05)), 2),
           .by = crsp_cl_grp) |>
    mutate(caldt     = ceiling_date(ym, "month") - days(1),
           age_years = as.numeric(caldt - first_offer) / 365.25) |>
    select(crsp_cl_grp, caldt, fund_name, n_class, tna, ret_vw, ret_ew, exp_ratio, mgmt_fee,
           actual_12b1, turn_ratio, first_offer, crsp_obj_cd, age_years)
}




Code
if (data_source == "crsp" && !file.exists(pq_path)) {
  message(pq_path, " not found; switching to the simulated panel.")
  data_source <- "simulated"
}

raw <- if (data_source == "crsp") read_parquet(pq_path) else simulate_clgrp(ff)

fund <- raw |>
  mutate(crsp_cl_grp = as.integer(crsp_cl_grp),

         across(c(exp_ratio, mgmt_fee, actual_12b1, turn_ratio), \(x) if_else(x < 0, NA_real_, x))) |>
  arrange(crsp_cl_grp, ym)

# One row per fund and calendar month, or every lag below is wrong
dup <- fund |> count(crsp_cl_grp, ym) |> filter(n > 1)
stopifnot("More than one row per class group and month" = nrow(dup) == 0)

last_month <- max(fund$ym)

fund_life <- fund |>
  summarise(first_ym = min(ym), last_ym = max(ym), months = n(),
            exits = max(ym) < last_month, .by = crsp_cl_grp)

cat("Data source:", data_source, "\n",
    "Funds (class groups):", n_distinct(fund$crsp_cl_grp), "\n",
    "Fund-months:         ", format(nrow(fund), big.mark = ","), "\n",
    "Months:              ", format(min(fund$ym), "%Y-%m"), "to", format(last_month, "%Y-%m"), "\n",

  summarise(tna_med = median(tna, na.rm = TRUE), age = median(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
text:
2. What Is a Flow?

2.1 Definition
TNA changes because the assets earn a return and because investors buy or redeem shares. The flow is what is left after the return is taken out. The dollar flow of fund \(i\) in month \(t\) is
\[
F_{i,t} = \text{TNA}_{i,t} - \text{TNA}_{i,t-1}\,(1 + R_{i,t}),
\tag{2}
\]
and the percentage flow, the measure used by Sirri and Tufano (1998), Chevalier and Ellison (1997), and most of the literature, scales it by lagged TNA:
\[
\text{Flow}_{i,t} = \frac{\text{TNA}_{i,t} - \text{TNA}_{i,t-1}\,(1 + R_{i,t})}{\text{TNA}_{i,t-1}}.
\tag{3}
\]
Equation (3) carries an assumption about timing: all of month \(t\)’s flow arrives at the end of the month, so it earns none of month \(t\)’s return. If money arrived at the start of the month instead, the flow would be \(\text{TNA}_{i,t}/(1+R_{i,t}) - \text{TNA}_{i,t-1}\). At a monthly frequency the two are close; over a year they are not (§2.6).
Because \(R_{i,t}\) is the CRSP total return, which assumes distributions are reinvested, a distribution that investors take in cash rather than reinvest leaves the fund and shows up as an outflow. Funds that pay large year-end capital-gain distributions will therefore show December outflows that have nothing to do with investors’ views of performance.


2.2 From share classes to the fund
We measure flows at the fund level, using the class-group TNA and the value-weighted return ret_vw. Aggregation helps and hurts.
It helps because the most common non-flow in share-class data disappears: investors who move from one share class to another (for example, C shares converting to A shares after some years) create an outflow in one class and an equal inflow in another, which net out in the fund total. Tiny share classes no longer have their own explosive percentage flows.
It hurts in two ways that are easy to miss.

Share-class launches and closures. When a fund adds a class, the new class’s first-month assets enter fund TNA. If the money is new, it is a genuine inflow; if it was seeded by the sponsor or moved from another fund, it is not. Months in which n_class changes are the place to look.
A missing share class. Fund TNA is the sum of the class TNAs that are reported. If one class’s TNA is missing for a month, fund TNA drops by that class’s assets and comes back the next month. Equation (3) records an outflow followed by an equal inflow. Because n_class counts share-class records rather than non-missing TNAs, it does not reveal this; the signature is a pair of offsetting dollar flows.

The return has its own aggregation detail: ret_vw weights by lagged class TNA, so it is missing in a fund’s first month and in any month in which no class has a lagged TNA. ret_ew exists in those months, but using it would change the weights of the return that Equation (3) subtracts.


Code
diag <- fund |>
  group_by(crsp_cl_grp) |>
  mutate(consec       = !is.na(lag(ym)) & lag(ym) == ym %m-% months(1),
         class_change = consec & n_class != lag(n_class)) |>
  ungroup()

tibble(
  Issue = c("Fund-months",
            "Previous calendar month missing (first month or a gap)",
            "ret_vw missing",
            "... of which ret_ew is available",
            "TNA missing",
            "TNA below $15M",
            "Number of share classes changes from last month"),
  `Fund-months` = c(nrow(diag),
                    sum(!diag$consec),
                    sum(is.na(diag$ret_vw)),
                    sum(is.na(diag$ret_vw) & !is.na(diag$ret_ew)),
                    sum(is.na(diag$tna)),
                    sum(diag$tna < 15, na.rm = TRUE),
                    sum(diag$class_change)),
  Funds = c(n_distinct(diag$crsp_cl_grp),
            n_distinct(diag$crsp_cl_grp[!diag$consec]),
            n_distinct(diag$crsp_cl_grp[is.na(diag$ret_vw)]),
            n_distinct(diag$crsp_cl_grp[is.na(diag$ret_vw) & !is.na(diag$ret_ew)]),
            n_distinct(diag$crsp_cl_grp[is.na(diag$tna)]),
            n_distinct(diag$crsp_cl_grp[coalesce(diag$tna < 15, FALSE)]),
            n_distinct(diag$crsp_cl_grp[diag$class_change]))
) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(`Fund-months`, Funds), decimals = 0) |>
  tab_header(title = "Data Checks Before Computing a Single Flow")

                dashStyle = "ShortDash", color = "#555555") |>

Figure 1: Number of funds reporting each month, and the cross-sectional distribution of fund TNA




The number of funds reporting is not constant: funds enter the panel when they are launched (or when their class group first appears in CRSP) and leave when they are merged or liquidated. Because every fund must have ten years of returns, entries are concentrated early in the sample and exits late.


2.3 Computing monthly flows
A flow in month \(t\) requires a row in month \(t\) and in month \(t-1\), a fund return in \(t\), and TNA in both months. We apply the requirements one at a time and count what survives.


Code
flows <- fund |>
  group_by(crsp_cl_grp) |>
  mutate(tna_lag     = lag(tna),
         n_class_lag = lag(n_class),
         consec      = !is.na(lag(ym)) & lag(ym) == ym %m-% months(1)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(dflow        = tna - tna_lag * (1 + ret_vw),         # Equation (2), $ millions
         flow         = dflow / tna_lag,                      # Equation (3)
         class_change = consec & n_class != n_class_lag)

attr_steps <- list(
  "0. All fund-months"                              = rep(TRUE, nrow(flows)),
  "1. Previous calendar month present"              = flows$consec,
  "2. ... and fund return (ret_vw) this month"      = flows$consec & !is.na(flows$ret_vw),
  "3. ... and TNA in both months (lagged TNA > 0)"  = flows$consec & !is.na(flows$ret_vw) &
                                                       !is.na(flows$tna) & coalesce(flows$tna_lag > 0, FALSE),
  "4. ... and lagged TNA >= $15M"                   = flows$consec & !is.na(flows$ret_vw) &
                                                       !is.na(flows$tna) & coalesce(flows$tna_lag >= 15, FALSE)
)

attr_tbl <- imap(attr_steps, \(keep, nm)
  tibble(step = nm, months = sum(keep), funds = n_distinct(flows$crsp_cl_grp[keep]))) |>
  list_rbind()

Step 4 applies the $15 million size filter of Lecture 3 to the lagged TNA, because lagged TNA is the denominator of Equation (3). Unlike in the share-class data, it is applied to the whole fund, as it should be.


2.4 Small denominators and extreme flows


Code
valid <- flows |> filter(consec, !is.na(ret_vw), !is.na(tna), coalesce(tna_lag > 0, FALSE))

valid |>
  mutate(size = cut(tna_lag, c(0, 15, 100, Inf), right = FALSE,
                    labels = c("Below $15M", "$15M to $100M", "$100M and above"))) |>
  summarise(n    = n(),
            p01  = quantile(flow, .01), p50 = median(flow), p99 = quantile(flow, .99),
            min  = min(flow), max = max(flow), sd = sd(flow),
            .by = size) |>
  arrange(size) |>

The percentage flows of a reversal are not symmetric (a 40% drop is undone by a 67% rise), which is why the check is done in dollars. These pairs make measured flows negatively autocorrelated and inflate their variance without carrying any information about investors. Two fixes are available: add the count of share classes with non-missing TNA to the aggregation step, and drop months in which that count changes; or, as here, flag reversals and check them by hand.






ImportantWhat a flow is not



Equation (3) attributes to “investor flows” every change in TNA not explained by the return. Six other things also change TNA:

Mergers. The surviving fund gains the target’s assets in one month; the target disappears.
Share-class launches. Seed money and assets moved from elsewhere arrive as an “inflow”.
Share-class conversions. They net out at the fund level, which is one reason to aggregate.
Missing class TNA. A one-month gap in one class’s TNA produces a reversal pair.
Cash distributions. Distributions not reinvested appear as outflows (§2.1).
Liquidations. A fund being wound down shows a final collapse in TNA, and often its last flow is never recorded (§4.5, §5).



We use the filtered sample from here on, drop the flagged reversal months, and winsorize flows at the 1st and 99th percentiles to limit the influence of the remaining extreme months.


Code
winsor <- function(x, p = 0.01) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(p, 1 - p), na.rm = TRUE)
  pmin(pmax(x, q[1]), q[2])
}

rev_keys <- reversals |>
  transmute(crsp_cl_grp, ym) |>
  bind_rows(reversals |> transmute(crsp_cl_grp, ym = ym %m+% months(1)))   # both months of a pair

clean <- clean |>
  anti_join(rev_keys, by = c("crsp_cl_grp", "ym")) |>
  mutate(flow_w = winsor(flow)) |>
  group_by(crsp_cl_grp) |>
  mutate(flow_lag = if_else(lag(ym) == ym %m-% months(1), lag(flow_w), NA_real_)) |>
  ungroup()

cat("Filtered sample:", format(nrow(clean), big.mark = ","), "fund-months from",
    n_distinct(clean$crsp_cl_grp), "funds\n",
    "Winsorization bounds (monthly flow):",
    paste(scales::percent(range(clean$flow_w), accuracy = 0.1), collapse = " to "), "\n")

2.5 Flows over time
Before asking how flows respond to each fund’s performance, look at what the sample’s funds as a group experienced. The aggregate flow rate in month \(t\) is total dollar flow over total lagged TNA, \(\sum_i F_{i,t} / \sum_i \text{TNA}_{i,t-1}\); we add up the twelve monthly rates in each calendar year.


Code
agg <- clean |>
  summarise(rate = sum(dflow) / sum(tna_lag), .by = ym) |>
  mutate(year = year(ym)) |>
  summarise(rate = 100 * sum(rate), months = n(), .by = year) |>
  arrange(year)

hchart(agg, "column", hcaes(x = year, y = round(rate, 2))) |>
  hc_chart(height = 340) |>
  hc_title(text = "Net flows into the sample funds, by year") |>
  hc_xAxis(title = list(text = NULL)) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Aggregate flow (% of assets per year)"),
           plotLines = list(list(value = 0, color = "#999999", width = 1))) |>
  hc_plotOptions(column = list(negativeColor = "#C0392B")) |>
  hc_legend(enabled = FALSE) |>
  hc_tooltip(pointFormat = "Flow: <b>{point.y:.1f}%</b> of assets")








Figure 2: Aggregate annual flow rate of the sample funds (sum of monthly dollar flows over lagged TNA)




The level of these flows is not the subject of this lecture: it reflects the industry-wide move from active funds to index funds and ETFs documented in Lecture 3 (Dannhauser and Pontiff 2026), and it is absorbed by time fixed effects in every regression below. What we study is how flows are distributed across funds within a period.


2.6 From monthly to annual flows
Sirri and Tufano (1998) measure flows at the annual frequency, from year-end TNA. Applying Equation (3) to a year and adding up twelve monthly dollar flows are not the same thing. If \(F_s\) is the dollar flow in month \(s\) of the year,
\[
\text{TNA}_{\text{Dec}} - \text{TNA}_{\text{Dec}-1}\prod_{s=1}^{12}(1+R_s)
= \sum_{s=1}^{12} F_s \prod_{u=s+1}^{12}(1+R_u).
\tag{4}
\]
The annual formula counts as “flow” not only the new money but also the return that new money earned for the rest of the year. In a year with high returns and early inflows, the annual measure is larger than the sum of the monthly flows. A second, more important difference: the annual formula needs a December TNA, so a fund that disappears during the year has no annual flow at all, while the sum of its monthly flows up to its last month is perfectly well defined. §4.5 shows why this matters.


Code
# Calendar-year panel: December TNA, 12-month return, Dec-to-Dec flow, and summed monthly flows
monthly_all <- valid |> mutate(year = year(ym))

dec <- fund |>
  filter(month(ym) == 12) |>
  transmute(crsp_cl_grp, year = year(ym), tna_dec = tna, age_dec = age_years,
            er_dec = exp_ratio, b12_dec = actual_12b1, obj_dec = crsp_obj_cd)

yr_ret <- fund |>
  mutate(year = year(ym)) |>
  summarise(n_ret = sum(!is.na(ret_vw)), ret_y = prod(1 + ret_vw) - 1,
            vol_y = sd(ret_vw), .by = c(crsp_cl_grp, year)) |>
  mutate(ret_y = if_else(n_ret == 12, ret_y, NA_real_),
         vol_y = if_else(n_ret == 12, vol_y, NA_real_))

yr_flow <- fund |>
  mutate(year = year(ym)) |>
  summarise(rows = n(), .by = c(crsp_cl_grp, year)) |>
  left_join(monthly_all |> summarise(n_flow = n(), sum_dflow = sum(dflow), .by = c(crsp_cl_grp, year)),
            by = c("crsp_cl_grp", "year")) |>
  mutate(complete_year = coalesce(n_flow, 0L) == rows)    # every month the fund existed has a flow

annual <- yr_ret |>
  left_join(dec, by = c("crsp_cl_grp", "year")) |>
  left_join(yr_flow, by = c("crsp_cl_grp", "year")) |>
  left_join(fund_life |> select(crsp_cl_grp, last_ym, exits), by = "crsp_cl_grp") |>
  arrange(crsp_cl_grp, year) |>
  group_by(crsp_cl_grp) |>
  mutate(prev_ok     = lag(year) == year - 1,
         tna_dec_lag = if_else(prev_ok, lag(tna_dec), NA_real_)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(exit_year   = exits & year == year(last_ym),
         flow_annual = (tna_dec - tna_dec_lag * (1 + ret_y)) / tna_dec_lag,   # Dec-to-Dec, Eq. (3)
         flow_summed = if_else(complete_year, sum_dflow / tna_dec_lag, NA_real_))

  filter(!is.na(flow_annual), !is.na(flow_summed), tna_dec_lag >= 15) |>
  mutate(x = round(100 * flow_summed, 2), y = round(100 * flow_annual, 2))
lim <- range(c(annual_plot$x, annual_plot$y))

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
section: 3. Why Should Flows Respond to Performance?
text:
3. Why Should Flows Respond to Performance?

3.1 The rational benchmark
Investors cannot observe a manager’s skill, but they can observe returns. In Berk and Green (2004), investors update their beliefs about skill after each return and move money toward managers who look skilled. Two further assumptions close the model: skill has decreasing returns to scale, and capital is supplied competitively. Money then flows to a good manager until the expected net alpha of the marginal dollar is zero. Three implications are worth keeping:

Flows respond strongly to past performance, even though past performance does not predict future net returns. Chasing performance is rational in the model, and the absence of persistence is its consequence, not evidence against it.
The response is larger for young funds, because each return is more informative when there is less history.
Skill shows up in size, not in net alpha, which is why Lecture 2 measured skill in dollars of value added (Berk and Binsbergen 2015).

Early evidence that flows follow past performance predates the model (Ippolito 1992). The question that occupies the literature is the shape of the response, and which performance investors respond to.


3.2 Convexity and costly search
Sirri and Tufano (1998) estimate annual flows of equity funds as a piecewise-linear function of the fund’s performance rank. They find a convex relationship: funds in the top performance quintile receive large inflows, while funds in the bottom quintiles lose comparatively little. Their explanation is search costs. Investors find it costly to evaluate many funds, so they buy the visible ones, and visibility (media attention, advertising, star ratings) is concentrated on top performers. Investors in poorly performing funds, meanwhile, face their own frictions in leaving.
Three papers refine the explanation:

Chevalier and Ellison (1997) estimate the shape of the flow–performance relationship semiparametrically and show that it gives managers an incentive to change the riskiness of the portfolio late in the year, depending on the year-to-date return. They find that funds do change their risk between September and December in the predicted direction. The shape is an incentive; the next lecture studies the behavior it induces.
Huang et al. (2007) model investors who learn about skill and pay participation costs. Funds with lower participation costs (for example, those in large families or with wider distribution) have higher flow sensitivity to medium performance and lower sensitivity to high performance than funds with higher participation costs.
Lynch and Musto (2003) argue that the weak response to poor performance is rational: funds tend to change strategy after poor returns, and the past returns of a strategy that has been abandoned say little about the future. Their evidence supports both predictions: strategy changes follow poor performance, and poor performers that change strategy have flows that are less sensitive to past returns.



3.3 Which performance do investors respond to?
If flows reflect learning about skill, investors should respond to a risk-adjusted measure. Three papers use flows to infer which measure, with conflicting answers.

Berk and Binsbergen (2016) rank asset pricing models by how well the sign of each model’s alpha predicts the sign of flows. The CAPM wins, beating no adjustment and the multi-factor models.
Barber et al. (2016) decompose returns into alpha and factor-related returns and ask which components flows respond to. Investors attend most to market risk: they discount returns due to market beta, but treat returns due to size, value, momentum, and industry exposures largely as alpha. More sophisticated investors use more sophisticated benchmarks.
Evans and Sun (2021) use the 2002 change in Morningstar’s rating methodology, which began comparing funds within size and value categories, as a natural experiment. Before the change, retail flows track CAPM alphas; after it, they respond more to Fama-French three-factor alphas. Institutional flows track three-factor alphas throughout. A better heuristic made retail investors look more sophisticated.
Ben-David et al. (2022) argue that investors do not use the CAPM at all. Morningstar ratings and recent returns explain flows better than any model’s alpha, flows do not adjust for market beta, and the earlier CAPM results come from the correlation between alphas and ratings and from how pooled regressions weight extreme market periods.

The common thread: the performance measure investors respond to is shaped by what is shown to them. For empirical work, this means the choice of performance measure in a flow regression is a hypothesis about investors, and it should be tested, not assumed.


3.4 The shape is not universal

Evidence on the shape of the flow–performance relationship







Setting
Finding
Source




U.S. equity mutual funds
Convex: top performers gain much more than poor performers lose
Sirri and Tufano (1998)


Pension fund managers
Clients withdraw from poor performers but do not disproportionately reward winners
Del Guercio and Tkac (2002)


Corporate bond funds
Concave: outflows respond more to poor performance than inflows to good performance; stronger when assets are illiquid
Goldstein et al. (2017)


28 countries
Shape varies by country; in more developed markets investors sell losers more and buy winners less
Ferreira et al. (2012)


Market states
Sensitivity is hump-shaped in aggregate factor realizations: weaker when factor returns are large
Franzoni and Schmalz (2017)


Active funds, index funds, ETFs
Performance chasing in all three vehicles; ETFs most sensitive
Dannhauser and Pontiff (2026)


Specification
Convexity in percentage flows disappears when heterogeneity is controlled for or flows are measured as changes in market share
Spiegel and Zhang (2013)



Two patterns stand out. First, the shape depends on the clientele: pension sponsors, who evaluate managers in committee and against benchmarks, punish losers but do not chase winners (Del Guercio and Tkac 2002). Second, it depends on liquidity: in corporate bond funds, an investor who redeems early avoids the cost of the fire sales that later redemptions force, so outflows respond strongly to poor performance and the relationship becomes concave (Goldstein et al. 2017). The convex shape that the tournament literature takes as given is a feature of retail equity funds in the United States, not a law.

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
section: 4. Estimating Flow–Performance Sensitivity in the Ten-Fund Sample
text:
4. Estimating Flow–Performance Sensitivity in the Ten-Fund Sample

4.1 Performance measures from public data
The canonical design ranks each fund against all funds with the same objective in the same year. Ten share classes are not a peer group: a fund ranked first of ten in our file could rank anywhere in the universe. We therefore measure performance against an external benchmark, the market, and use the variation within each share class over time.
For each share-class-month \(t\) we compute three measures over the twelve months \(t-12\) to \(t-1\):

Raw return \(R^{(12)}_{i,t}\): the compounded return.
Market-adjusted return \(R^{(12)}_{i,t} - R^{(12)}_{m,t}\): the compounded fund return minus the compounded market return.
CAPM alpha: \(\sum_{s=t-12}^{t-1}\bigl[(R_{i,s} - R_{f,s}) - \hat\beta_{i}\,(R_{m,s} - R_{f,s})\bigr]\), with \(\hat\beta_i\) estimated over months \(t-48\) to \(t-13\) (at least 24 months). Estimating beta before the performance window keeps the window’s returns out of the beta, in the spirit of Barber et al. (2016).

Performance always ends in month \(t-1\), so the month-\(t\) return, which enters the flow through Equation (3), is never on both sides of the regression.


Code
roll_sum <- function(x, k) as.numeric(stats::filter(x, rep(1, k), sides = 1))   # sum of last k values

perf <- panel |>
  select(crsp_fundno, ym, ret) |>
  group_by(crsp_fundno) |>
  complete(ym = seq(min(ym), max(ym), by = "month")) |>        # explicit NA for skipped months
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(ff, by = "ym") |>
  arrange(crsp_fundno, ym) |>
  group_by(crsp_fundno) |>
  mutate(
    exr    = ret - rf,
    ret12  = expm1(lag(roll_sum(log1p(ret), 12))),              # months t-12 ... t-1
    mkt12  = expm1(lag(roll_sum(log1p(mktrf + rf), 12))),
    adj12  = ret12 - mkt12,
    # rolling CAPM beta over 36 months, at least 24 valid
    ok     = !is.na(exr) & !is.na(mktrf),
    x0     = if_else(ok, mktrf, 0), y0 = if_else(ok, exr, 0),
    n36    = roll_sum(ok, 36),
    beta36 = (roll_sum(x0 * y0, 36) - roll_sum(x0, 36) * roll_sum(y0, 36) / n36) /
             (roll_sum(x0^2, 36)    - roll_sum(x0, 36)^2 / n36),
    beta36 = if_else(n36 >= 24, beta36, NA_real_),
    beta_pre = lag(beta36, 13),                                 # estimated through t-13
    alpha12  = lag(roll_sum(exr, 12)) - beta_pre * lag(roll_sum(mktrf, 12))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(crsp_fundno, ym, ret12, adj12, alpha12, beta_pre)

fp <- clean |>
  left_join(perf, by = c("crsp_fundno", "ym")) |>
  filter(!is.na(ret12), !is.na(adj12), !is.na(alpha12), !is.na(flow_lag)) |>   # common sample
  mutate(log_tna_lag = log(tna_lag),
         ret_pos   = pmax(ret12, 0),  adj_pos = pmax(adj12, 0),  alpha_pos = pmax(alpha12, 0))

cat("Flow-performance sample:", nrow(fp), "share-class-months,",
    n_distinct(fp$crsp_fundno), "share classes,",
    format(min(fp$ym), "%Y-%m"), "to", format(max(fp$ym), "%Y-%m"), "\n")


Flow-performance sample: 1558 share-class-months, 8 share classes, 2004-01 to 2026-03 








WarningWhat ten share classes can and cannot tell us



This sample is a laboratory for the mechanics, not evidence on investor behavior. Three limits are worth stating before any number appears.

No peer ranks. Ranks within ten funds say nothing about where a fund stands in its objective class, which is what investors see.
Ten clusters. Standard errors clustered by fund are unreliable with ten clusters. We cluster by month, which allows for common shocks to all funds in a month but not for persistence within a fund; with overlapping twelve-month performance windows and persistent flows, the reported standard errors are too small.
Share classes, not funds. Flows to a share class include conversions between classes and depend on how the class is distributed, which varies across the ten.





4.2 The pooled regression
We estimate monthly flows on past performance with share-class fixed effects:
\[
\text{Flow}_{i,t} = a_i + b\,P_{i,t} + k\,\max(P_{i,t}, 0) + \gamma' X_{i,t-1} + \varepsilon_{i,t},
\tag{5}
\]
where \(P_{i,t}\) is one of the three performance measures and \(X_{i,t-1}\) holds the log of lagged TNA and the lagged flow. The slope is \(b\) for underperformance and \(b + k\) for outperformance, so \(k\) is the kink: \(k > 0\) is convexity. Writing the regression this way puts the test of convexity in a single coefficient.


Code
fp_models <- list(
  "Linear"            = feols(flow_w ~ adj12 | crsp_fundno, fp, cluster = ~ym),
  "Kink"              = feols(flow_w ~ adj12 + adj_pos | crsp_fundno, fp, cluster = ~ym),
  "Kink + controls"   = feols(flow_w ~ adj12 + adj_pos + log_tna_lag + flow_lag | crsp_fundno, fp, cluster = ~ym),
  "Raw return"        = feols(flow_w ~ ret12 + ret_pos + log_tna_lag + flow_lag | crsp_fundno, fp, cluster = ~ym),
  "CAPM alpha"        = feols(flow_w ~ alpha12 + alpha_pos + log_tna_lag + flow_lag | crsp_fundno, fp, cluster = ~ym)
)

# A gt regression table: coefficient (stars) over (standard error)
reg_gt <- function(models, rows, title, subtitle = NULL) {
  stars <- function(p) case_when(p < .01 ~ "***", p < .05 ~ "**", p < .10 ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")
  body <- imap(models, \(m, nm) {
    ct <- coeftable(m)
    map(names(rows), \(v) {
      vv <- rows[[v]][rows[[v]] %in% rownames(ct)]
      if (length(vv) == 0) return(tibble(term = v, stat = c("b", "se"), value = ""))
      tibble(term = v, stat = c("b", "se"),
             value = c(sprintf("%.4f%s", ct[vv, 1], stars(ct[vv, 4])), sprintf("(%.4f)", ct[vv, 2])))
    }) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(model = nm)
  }) |> list_rbind()
  fit <- imap(models, \(m, nm) tibble(
    term = c("Observations", "Within R²"), stat = "b", model = nm,
    value = c(format(nobs(m), big.mark = ","), sprintf("%.3f", fitstat(m, "wr2")[[1]])))) |> list_rbind()
  bind_rows(body, fit) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = value) |>
    mutate(term = if_else(stat == "se", "", term)) |>
    select(-stat) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(term = "") |>
    tab_header(title = title, subtitle = subtitle) |>
    tab_source_note("Share-class fixed effects in all columns. Standard errors clustered by month. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.")
}

The coefficients are per unit of annual performance and the flow is monthly: a coefficient of 0.01 means that a trailing return 10 percentage points higher goes with a monthly flow 0.1 percentage points higher, roughly 1.2% of assets over a year.
Read the table in three steps. The first column is the average sensitivity: how much a share class’s monthly flow moves with a one-unit change in its trailing twelve-month market-adjusted return. The second asks whether the slope is different above zero; a positive kink is convexity, and the size of the kink relative to its standard error is the test. The third column adds the two controls that every flow regression includes. Flows are persistent, and larger funds have smaller percentage flows. The last two columns repeat the third with raw returns and CAPM alphas, in the spirit of Berk and Binsbergen (2016) and Barber et al. (2016): the measure with the higher within-\(R^2\) explains more of the variation in flows. With ten share classes, the differences between measures are small and should not be over-read.


4.3 What the regression is fitting
A binned scatter shows the data behind the regression. We remove each share class’s average flow, sort the months into ten bins of market-adjusted performance, and plot the average flow in each bin, with the fitted line from the kink regression.


Code

binned <- fp |>
  mutate(flow_dm = flow_w - mean(flow_w), .by = crsp_fundno) |>
  mutate(bin = ntile(adj12, 10)) |>
  summarise(x = mean(adj12), y = mean(flow_dm), .by = bin) |>
  arrange(bin)

kink_fit <- function(x) b_kink[["adj12"]] * x + b_kink[["adj_pos"]] * pmax(x, 0)
level    <- -mean(kink_fit(fp$adj12))            # demeaned flows average zero over the sample
fit_line <- tibble(x = seq(quantile(fp$adj12, .01), quantile(fp$adj12, .99), length.out = 200)) |>
  mutate(y = level + kink_fit(x))

  hc_chart(height = 420) |>
  hc_title(text = "Flows and past performance, ten share classes") |>

  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Monthly flow, demeaned (%)")) |>
  hc_add_series(binned |> mutate(x = 100 * x, y = 100 * y), "scatter",
                hcaes(x = x, y = y), name = "Decile averages", marker = list(radius = 6)) |>
  hc_add_series(fit_line |> mutate(x = 100 * x, y = 100 * y), "line",
                hcaes(x = x, y = y), name = "Kink regression", marker = list(enabled = FALSE)) |>

4.4 Fund by fund
The pooled regression imposes one sensitivity on all share classes. With a long monthly history per class, we can instead estimate a sensitivity for each, using Newey-West standard errors because the twelve-month performance windows overlap.


Code
fp_t <- fp |> mutate(t = interval(min(ym), ym) %/% months(1))

by_fund <- fp_t |>
  filter(n() >= 36, .by = crsp_fundno) |>
  group_split(crsp_fundno) |>
  map(\(d) {
    m  <- feols(flow_w ~ adj12, d, panel.id = ~crsp_fundno + t, vcov = NW(12))
    ct <- coeftable(m)
    tibble(fund = as.character(d$crsp_fundno[1]), n = nobs(m),
           b = ct["adj12", 1], se = ct["adj12", 2])
  }) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(lo = b - 1.96 * se, hi = b + 1.96 * se) |>
  arrange(b)




Code
highchart() |>
  hc_chart(height = 400) |>
  hc_title(text = "One sensitivity per share class") |>
  hc_xAxis(categories = by_fund$fund, title = list(text = "crsp_fundno")) |>
  hc_yAxis(title = list(text = "Monthly flow per unit of 12-month market-adjusted return"),
           plotLines = list(list(value = 0, color = "#999999", width = 1),
                            list(value = coef(fp_models[["Linear"]])[["adj12"]], color = "#C0392B",
                                 width = 1, dashStyle = "Dash",
                                 label = list(text = "Pooled estimate", align = "right")))) |>
  hc_add_series(name = "Estimate", type = "scatter", data = round(by_fund$b, 4),
                marker = list(radius = 6)) |>
  hc_add_series(name = "95% CI", type = "errorbar",
                data = map2(round(by_fund$lo, 4), round(by_fund$hi, 4), \(l, h) list(l, h))) |>
  hc_tooltip(shared = TRUE, valueDecimals = 3)








Figure 5: Flow–performance sensitivity by share class, with 95% confidence intervals (Newey-West, 12 lags)




The point estimates vary widely across share classes, and the intervals are wide. Two lessons follow. A pooled sensitivity is an average over heterogeneous investors: a retail share class sold through brokers and an institutional class held by a few large clients can face very different flow functions. And, as Spiegel and Zhang (2013) point out, pooling heterogeneous linear responses can produce a pooled shape that no single fund has. Section 5 makes this concrete.

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
section: 5. Is the Convexity Real? Three Simulations

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
text:
6. Why the Shape Matters
For managers. A convex flow function is an option on performance: the fund company gains a lot from a top rank and loses little from a bottom one, so the value of the option rises with risk. Chevalier and Ellison (1997) show that the shape of the flow function predicts how funds change their risk late in the year. The next lecture tests this tournament behavior directly, and shows how fragile the tests are.
For equilibrium. In Berk and Green (2004), flows are the mechanism that drives net alpha to zero. Whether flows respond to the right performance measure (§3.3) decides how efficiently capital is allocated across managers.
For prices. Flows force trades. Funds with large outflows sell their holdings at the same time, and the stocks they hold in common fall in price before recovering (Coval and Stafford 2007). Flow-induced purchases can push up the prices of stocks that funds already own, which in turn raises the funds’ returns and attracts more flows, a mechanism Lou (2012) links to the persistence of fund performance and to stock price momentum.
For investors. Whether flows are “smart” is itself debated. New money appears to flow to funds that subsequently do well (Gruber 1996; Zheng 1999), but over longer horizons, the stocks that fund investors buy underperform (Frazzini and Lamont 2008). Week 8 takes up the behavioral side.
For fragility. Where investors who leave early impose costs on those who stay, as in less liquid bond funds, the flow function becomes concave and redemptions can feed on themselves (Goldstein et al. 2017).

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
text:
7. A Checklist for Flow Studies

Choose the unit. Measure flows at the fund level (class group or portfolio), so that share-class conversions net out. Aggregate TNA by summing and returns with lagged-TNA weights.
Check the panel. One row per fund and calendar month; never take “the previous row” as “the previous month”.
Know what aggregation creates. Flag months in which the number of share classes changes, and record how many classes report TNA; a missing class produces a reversal pair.
Clean the characteristics. Negative values in CRSP expense ratios and similar fields are missing-value codes.
Filter on the denominator. Apply a minimum lagged TNA ($15 million is common) at the fund level.
Read the extremes. Inspect the largest flows by hand. Mergers, share-class launches, and reporting gaps are not investor decisions.
Winsorize, and report the bounds. Percentage flows have very fat tails even after filtering.
Keep the dying funds. Use monthly data to record the flows of funds that exit before year-end; an annual sample of year-end survivors truncates the bottom of the flow function. Ask whether the sample itself was selected on survival.
Use lagged performance. The month-\(t\) return enters the month-\(t\) flow; performance should end at \(t-1\).
Rank deliberately. Ranks within a sample estimate ranks in the population with error; ranks within objective codes need enough funds per code.
Test the performance measure. Raw return, CAPM alpha, multi-factor alpha, and Morningstar ratings are competing hypotheses about investors (Berk and Binsbergen 2016; Barber et al. 2016; Ben-David et al. 2022).
Allow for heterogeneity. Estimate the flow function within groups (age, size, clientele, distribution channel) before concluding that it is convex (Spiegel and Zhang 2013).
Cluster appropriately. Flows are persistent within funds and correlated across funds within periods; cluster by both.

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
text:
8. Key Takeaways

The flow function is the fund company’s incentive contract. Revenue is fee times TNA, and flows are how TNA responds to performance.
A flow is a residual. Equation (3) attributes to investors every change in TNA not explained by the return, including mergers, share-class launches, reporting gaps, cash distributions, and liquidations. Most of the work in measuring flows is removing what is not investor demand.
Aggregating to the fund removes some problems and creates others. Conversions between share classes net out; class launches and missing class TNA do not.
The standard finding is convexity (Sirri and Tufano 1998), explained by search costs and visibility, and refined by participation costs (Huang et al. 2007) and strategy changes after poor performance (Lynch and Musto 2003).
Investors respond to what they are shown. The evidence on CAPM, factor-adjusted, and rating-based performance (Berk and Binsbergen 2016; Barber et al. 2016; Evans and Sun 2021; Ben-David et al. 2022) says that the performance measure in a flow regression is a hypothesis about investors.
The shape depends on the clientele, the asset class, and the market state (Del Guercio and Tkac 2002; Goldstein et al. 2017; Ferreira et al. 2012; Franzoni and Schmalz 2017).
Estimated convexity can be manufactured. Dropping the flows of funds that exit, and pooling heterogeneous linear responses, both produce convex pooled estimates from linear investors (Spiegel and Zhang 2013). Ask what your estimate would look like if every investor were linear, and what your sample selection rule did to the funds at the bottom.

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
text:
9. Discussion Questions

Equation (3) assumes flows arrive at the end of the month. Derive the flow under the assumption that they arrive at the start of the month. Compute both versions for the 100 funds. For which funds and months does the choice matter most?
A fund pays a large capital-gain distribution in December and most investors reinvest it. Does Equation (3) record an outflow? What if most investors take it in cash? Using the monthly flows, check whether December flows in the sample look different from other months.
The aggregation step in make_fund_sample.R sums the TNA of the share classes that report in a month. Modify it to also count the share classes with non-missing TNA, and redo Table 7 using months in which that count changes. How many of the flagged reversals does the new variable explain?
Pick the largest inflow in Table 5. List the possible explanations and, for each one, a piece of CRSP data that would confirm or rule it out.
make_fund_sample.R requires 120 months of returns. Re-draw the sample with a 36-month requirement. Which results in Section 4 would you expect to change, and in which direction? Check the Low segment and the young-fund slopes in particular.
In Table 12, which ranking explains flows best? Is the difference large relative to what you would expect from chance? Design a test that accounts for the high correlation between the rankings (Table 9).
Berk and Binsbergen (2016) conclude that investors use the CAPM; Ben-David et al. (2022) conclude that they use Morningstar ratings and past returns. Using only the variables in this sample, which feature of the data would you exploit to distinguish the two views? What extra data would make the test sharp?
In Table 16, adding exit years changes the Low slope. Propose a way to bound the bias from funds whose final flows are never recorded at all, for example funds that exit between two monthly reports.
In experiment C, the convexity comes from where each clientele sits in the ranking. Modify simulate_industry() so that the market mostly falls. What shape does the pooled regression estimate now? Relate the answer to Franzoni and Schmalz (2017).
Funds with a 12b-1 fee are typically sold through intermediaries. Estimate the annual flow–performance regression separately for funds with and without a 12b-1 fee. Which theory in §3.2 would predict a difference, and in which direction?
Ferreira et al. (2012) find that the shape of the flow–performance relationship differs across countries. What would you expect for Taiwanese equity funds, and why? What data would you need, and which of the measurement problems in Section 2 would be most severe?

title: Lecture 4: Fund Flows and the Flow–Performance Relationship
text:
4. The Flow–Performance Relationship in 100 Funds

4.1 Performance measures and ranks
Sirri and Tufano (1998) rank each fund against the other funds in the same period, because a rank is closer to what an investor sees in a fund table or a rating than a raw number. With 100 funds drawn at random from one population, a fund’s rank among the sample funds is an estimate of its rank in the population of active domestic equity funds.






WarningHow good is a rank among 100 funds?



If \(p\) is a fund’s true percentile in the population and \(n\) funds are drawn at random, the fund’s percentile in the sample has a standard error of about \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\): roughly 5 percentile points at the median with \(n = 100\), and fewer in the tails. Our ranks therefore measure investors’ rankings with error, and errors in a regressor flatten the estimated slopes. The error is largest in the middle and smallest at the extremes, so it flattens the Mid segment more than the High segment, a small bias toward finding convexity. Ranking within CRSP objective codes, as many studies do, is not an option here: 100 funds spread across seven codes leaves too few funds per code and month.


We use three performance measures, all over a window that ends before the month whose flow we explain:

Raw return: the compounded return over the past twelve months (monthly design) or the previous calendar year (annual design).
CAPM alpha: \(\sum_{s=t-12}^{t-1}\bigl[(R_{i,s} - R_{f,s}) - \hat\beta_{i}\,(R_{m,s} - R_{f,s})\bigr]\), with \(\hat\beta_i\) estimated over months \(t-48\) to \(t-13\) (at least 24 months), in the spirit of Barber et al. (2016).
Three-factor alpha: the same with the Fama-French market, size, and value factors.

A market-adjusted return, \(R_i - R_m\), is not on the list. Within a month every fund is adjusted by the same market return, so it ranks funds exactly as the raw return does; it would differ only in a regression on levels without time fixed effects.


Code
# Realized CAPM and FF3 alphas over months t-12..t-1, betas from t-48..t-13 (>= 24 months)
alphas_one <- function(d) {
  n <- nrow(d); a1 <- a3 <- rep(NA_real_, n)
  X1 <- cbind(1, d$mktrf); X3 <- cbind(1, d$mktrf, d$smb, d$hml)
  if (n >= 49) for (t in 49:n) {
    est <- (t - 48):(t - 13); ev <- (t - 12):(t - 1)
    ok  <- !is.na(d$exr[est])
    if (sum(ok) < 24 || anyNA(d$exr[ev])) next
    b1 <- lm.fit(X1[est, , drop = FALSE][ok, , drop = FALSE], d$exr[est][ok])$coefficients
    b3 <- lm.fit(X3[est, , drop = FALSE][ok, , drop = FALSE], d$exr[est][ok])$coefficients
    a1[t] <- sum(d$exr[ev] - X1[ev, -1, drop = FALSE] %*% b1[-1])
    a3[t] <- sum(d$exr[ev] - X3[ev, -1, drop = FALSE] %*% b3[-1])
  }
  tibble(ym = d$ym, alpha_capm = a1, alpha_ff3 = a3)
}

roll_sum <- function(x, k) as.numeric(stats::filter(x, rep(1, k), sides = 1))   # sum of last k values

grid <- fund |>
  select(crsp_cl_grp, ym, ret_vw) |>
  group_by(crsp_cl_grp) |>
  complete(ym = seq(min(ym), max(ym), by = "month")) |>        # explicit NA for skipped months
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(ff, by = "ym") |>
  arrange(crsp_cl_grp, ym) |>
  mutate(exr = ret_vw - rf) |>
  group_by(crsp_cl_grp) |>
  mutate(ret12 = expm1(lag(roll_sum(log1p(ret_vw), 12)))) |>  # months t-12 ... t-1
  ungroup()

perf <- grid |>
  group_split(crsp_cl_grp) |>
  map(\(d) alphas_one(d) |> mutate(crsp_cl_grp = d$crsp_cl_grp[1])) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  right_join(grid |> select(crsp_cl_grp, ym, ret12), by = c("crsp_cl_grp", "ym")) |>
  # ranks among all sample funds with the measure in that month
  mutate(rank_ret  = if_else(is.na(ret12), NA_real_, percent_rank(ret12)),
         rank_capm = if_else(is.na(alpha_capm), NA_real_, percent_rank(alpha_capm)),
         rank_ff3  = if_else(is.na(alpha_ff3), NA_real_, percent_rank(alpha_ff3)),
         .by = ym)

perf |>

  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Measure", values_to = "Fund-months available") |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = 2, decimals = 0)

4.2 Replicating Sirri and Tufano (1998)
The Sirri and Tufano (1998) design is annual. For each fund-year we take the December-to-December flow of year \(y\) (Equation 3 at the annual frequency) and the fund’s fractional rank on its raw return in year \(y-1\), split into the three segments of Equation (6):
\[
\text{Flow}_{i,y} = \beta_L\,\text{Low}_{i,y-1} + \beta_M\,\text{Mid}_{i,y-1} + \beta_H\,\text{High}_{i,y-1} + \gamma' X_{i,y-1} + \delta_y + \varepsilon_{i,y},
\tag{6}
\]
with \(\text{Low} = \min(\text{Rank}, 0.2)\), \(\text{Mid} = \min(0.6, \text{Rank} - \text{Low})\), and \(\text{High} = \text{Rank} - \text{Low} - \text{Mid}\), so the pieces add up to the rank and each coefficient is the slope within one segment. Convexity means \(\beta_H > \beta_M\) and \(\beta_H > \beta_L\). The controls \(X\) are measured at the end of year \(y-1\): log TNA, log age, the expense ratio, the volatility of monthly returns, and, in the last column, the previous year’s flow. \(\delta_y\) is a year fixed effect, which absorbs the aggregate flows of §2.5. This is a stripped-down version of their specification, not a copy of it.


Code
rank_segments <- function(d, r = "rank") {
  d |> mutate(Low  = pmin(.data[[r]], 0.2),
              Mid  = pmin(0.6, pmax(.data[[r]] - 0.2, 0)),
              High = pmax(.data[[r]] - 0.8, 0))
}

# A gt regression table: coefficient (stars) over (standard error)
reg_gt <- function(models, rows, title, subtitle = NULL, note = NULL) {
  stars <- function(p) case_when(p < .01 ~ "***", p < .05 ~ "**", p < .10 ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")
  body <- imap(models, \(m, nm) {
    ct <- coeftable(m)
    map(names(rows), \(v) {
      vv <- rows[[v]][rows[[v]] %in% rownames(ct)]
      if (length(vv) == 0) return(tibble(term = v, stat = c("b", "se"), value = ""))
      tibble(term = v, stat = c("b", "se"),
             value = c(sprintf("%.3f%s", ct[vv, 1], stars(ct[vv, 4])), sprintf("(%.3f)", ct[vv, 2])))
    }) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(model = nm)
  }) |> list_rbind()
  fit <- imap(models, \(m, nm) tibble(
    term = c("Observations", "Within R²"), stat = "b", model = nm,
    value = c(format(nobs(m), big.mark = ","), sprintf("%.3f", fitstat(m, "wr2")[[1]])))) |> list_rbind()
  bind_rows(body, fit) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = value) |>
    mutate(term = if_else(stat == "se", "", term)) |>
    select(-stat) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(term = "") |>
    tab_header(title = title, subtitle = subtitle) |>
    tab_source_note(paste(note, "* p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
}

# Wald test of convexity: High slope minus Mid slope
convexity_test <- function(m, hi = "High", mid = "Mid") {
  b <- coef(m); V <- vcov(m)
  d <- b[[hi]] - b[[mid]]; se <- sqrt(V[hi, hi] + V[mid, mid] - 2 * V[hi, mid])
  tibble(diff = d, se = se, t = d / se)
}

The first two columns differ only through Equation (4), and should be close. The third adds the exit years. If exiting funds were poor performers with large outflows, adding them steepens the Low segment, and the gap between the bottom and the top of the flow function shrinks. With only a few dozen exit years among well over a thousand fund-years, expect a modest change; its direction is the point of §5’s experiment B, now in real data: a sample that measures flows only for funds alive at year-end understates how strongly investors leave losers. And this sample is already selected on ten years of survival, so the funds that would show this most strongly were never drawn.


4.6 One sensitivity per fund
The pooled regressions impose one flow function on all 100 funds. With a long monthly history per fund, we can instead estimate a sensitivity for each, regressing the monthly flow on the fund’s monthly rank (raw return), with Newey-West standard errors because the twelve-month windows behind consecutive ranks overlap.


Code
by_fund <- mp |>
  mutate(t = interval(min(ym), ym) %/% months(1)) |>
  filter(n() >= 60, .by = crsp_cl_grp) |>
  group_split(crsp_cl_grp) |>
  map(\(d) {
    m  <- feols(flow_w ~ rank_ret, d, panel.id = ~crsp_cl_grp + t, vcov = NW(12))
    ct <- coeftable(m)
    tibble(fund = as.character(d$crsp_cl_grp[1]), name = d$fund_name[nrow(d)], n = nobs(m),
           b = ct["rank_ret", 1], se = ct["rank_ret", 2],
           log_tna = mean(d$log_tna_lag), b12 = mean(coalesce(d$actual_12b1, 0) > 0))
  }) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(lo = b - 1.96 * se, hi = b + 1.96 * se) |>
  arrange(b)

pooled_b <- coef(feols(flow_w ~ rank_ret | crsp_cl_grp, mp))[["rank_ret"]]

Compare the last two columns. If the dispersion of the estimates across funds is about the size of the average standard error, most of what the chart shows is sampling noise.
